#6437. The Best Nontoxic Cookware Trusted by BA Editors (2026)

If you’ve shopped for nonstick pots and pans in the past decade, you’ve had the term nontoxic cookware thrown at you with increasing velocity. As you've thought about getting new pans you may have even searched for the best nontoxic cookware without being totally sure what “toxins” they supposedly do not have in them. So what exactly makes cookware “toxic,” and why do these “safe” or “healthy” pans claim to be better?

The answer begins with a class of synthetic chemicals known as PFAS, short for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances. These chemicals, which repel liquids, have been used in everything from waterproof jackets to nonstick cookware coatings, and after decades of use, the health concerns raised by scientists started to break through to the public more broadly in more recent years.

Whether you’ve never heard of PFAS or you’re already familiar with their nearly 100-year-old history, you’re in the right place if you want to avoid them. We’ve tested dozens of nonstick and “nontoxic” pans to find the best options to help you keep PFAS out of your cookware. Read on for the lowdown on all things nontoxic cookware.

When companies label their cookware “nontoxic,” it’s a marketing move as much as anything, designed to position it as a safer alternative to traditional nonstick, which is typically coated in a chemical called polytetrafluoroethylene, or PTFE. And to understand why people began to colloquially refer to old nonstick pans as “toxic,” we need a little history of PTFE.

Discovered accidentally in 1938 and trademarked by chemical company DuPont as Teflon in the early 1960s, PTFE was an earthquake in the home cookware market during the second half of the 20th century because it provided consumers with a completely nonstick, no-oil-needed cooking surface. By the turn of the century, Teflon had become ubiquitous, finding its way into a staggering number of American kitchens in the form of PTFE-coated skillets, muffin tins, baking dishes, and more.

PTFE, though, is just one of thousands of a class of chemicals in PFAS family mentioned earlier. Around 1951, DuPont started using another PFAS called PFOA (short for perfluorooctanoic acid) in its Teflon manufacturing process. Over time, it became clear that PFOA could enter the human body by way of gaseous fumes or chipped coatings and have detrimental effects on human health and the environment, including increased risk of certain cancers, birth defects, ulcerative colitis, and thyroid disease. Under mounting pressure from public health and environmental advocacy groups, manufacturers phased out PFOA by 2013.

These days traditional nonstick cookware is made using PFOA-free PTFE (which is also typically free of PFOS, another harmful PFAS). You’ll see it marketed under names like T-fal, Dura-Slide, or hard-anodized aluminum. While PTFE itself is considered less harmful than other PFAS, there is still a broader concern. Thousands of PFAS compounds remain unregulated, and there is ongoing research into the class of chemicals as a whole. A label that says “PFOA- and PFOS-free” does not necessarily mean the product is free of all potentially risky chemicals in the PFAS family.

While not necessarily the first recorded use of the term, the idea of “nontoxic” cookware was largely introduced to consumers when GreenPan released the first PFAS-free ceramic nonstick frying pans in 2007. Since then, “nontoxic cookware” has come to mean “PFAS-free nonstick cookware.” While there’s nothing inherently incorrect about this characterization, it’s important to recognize the degree to which it has become a marketing buzzword.

While “nontoxic cookware” typically refers to ceramic nonstick, which is made from silica using a method called the sol-gel process, any cookware that’s made without the use of harmful chemicals like PFAS can be considered “nontoxic.” That includes some tried-and-true options you probably already know and love: stainless steel, cast iron, and carbon steel.

Ceramic nonstick comes closest to mimicking the ease of traditional Teflon, but like any coating, it will degrade over time and can chip (more on that below). That’s why we recommend getting comfortable with uncoated stainless, cast iron, and carbon steel. With the right technique, your food won’t stick to them either, and they’ll last a lot longer.

Available sizes: 8", 10", 12"Induction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: Yes, but hand-washing recommendedMetal-utensil-safe: Theoretically, but wood or silicone recommendedOven-safe: Up to 600ºFWarranty: 1 year

About ceramic nonstick: I have to be honest here, I've personally sworn off coated nonstick pans for good, because no matter which one you buy, it will only last you a few years tops before the coating starts to degrade and you need to replace it. That said, I understand why people gravitate towards them—and if you're dead-set on buying one, ceramic nonstick is the way to go. These pans are typically made of stainless steel or aluminum and lined with a silica-based coating that makes them nice and slick—for a few years, at least. The exact makeup of that coating varies brand to brand, which is why we’ve spent years testing lots of ceramic nonstick pans to find the ones that best deliver on their nonstick promise.

Our top pick: GreenPan’s ceramic nonstick pans were the first to hit the market in 2007, and the brand’s products have consistently come out on top in our best nonstick pan testing. Its Valencia Pro line is our favorite for a few reasons: It’s hefty enough to feel durable while remaining lightweight enough to be easily maneuverable. It’s also affordable enough that you won’t have to break the bank when you inevitably need to replace it in a few years, and more scratch-resistant than some earlier GreenPan iterations we've tried. Oh, and it's induction compatible too.

A budget option: If you don’t cook on an induction stovetop and are looking for a cheaper option, you can go with GreenPan’s Paris Pro line, which performed similarly to the Valencia in our testing.

Read more about our favorite nonstick pans.

Deeper Carbon Nonstick Frying Pan & Glass Lid

Available sizes: 8", 10", 12"Induction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: NoMetal-utensil-safe: YesOven-safe: Up to 1,100ºFWarranty: Lifetime

About carbon nonstick (or nitrided carbon steel): At the outset, these pans act like traditional nonstick but can hold up to high heat, metal utensils, and years of use because they aren’t coated. Instead the carbon steel is nitrided, a process that infuses nitrogen into the metal to make it tougher, slicker, and both corrosion- and rust-resistant.

Our top pick: When we first got a hold of Misen’s Carbon Nonstick pan it seemed like the holy grail for anyone trying to quit Teflon without giving up easy-release eggs. Unlike traditional carbon steel pans, Misen’s version has an aluminum core that heats quickly and evenly, and its surface repels oil straight out of the box. In testing, fried eggs, chicken thighs, and sautéed onions all slid right off with minimal oil (food director Chris Morocco said it was “practically allergic” to eggs). The pan is lightweight and durable and will develop a terrific nonstick seasoning. However, as our lead cookware tester Wilder Davies continued cooking with the Misen, he noticed the initial corn oil seasoning layer started to wear, and the miraculous oil repelling characteristics decreased. Once that happened we assigned four more people, myself included, to work with these pans and we all noticed a reduction in the nonstickiness as time went on. However, the nonstick curve on these has proven to be more U-shaped, as we've continued to cook on and season them, food release started to become easier again.

Read our full review of the Misen Carbon Nonstick Pan.

D3 Stainless 3-ply Bonded Cookware; Saute Pan with lid; 3 quart

D3 Stainless Steel 14-in Skillet with Lid

Available sizes: 10", 12", 14"Induction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: NoMetal-utensil-safe: YesOven-safe: Up to 600°FWarranty: Limited lifetime

About stainless steel: Stainless-steel cookware is a staple in home and professional kitchens because of its versatility, durability, and low maintenance needs. Use it on the stovetop, in the oven, or with metal tools—unlike shorter-lived ceramic pans, a stainless-steel skillet can serve you well for a lifetime. And here’s the thing: With the proper technique, stainless steel can release almost as easily as ceramic nonstick. The key in guaranteeing your food slides right off instead of becoming a stuck-on mess is using sufficient fat and heat. Make sure to wait until your oil is shimmering before adding whatever you’re cooking, give it enough time in the pan to let the maillard reaction do its thing, and you should have no issues with stickage.

Our top pick: We’ve tested many types of stainless-steel cookware throughout the years here at BA, and one brand has repeatedly stood out time and time again for its consistently well-made, durable, high-performing products. That brand is All-Clad.

In our testing of stainless-steel frying pans and sauté pans, product testers and Test Kitchen editors alike lauded All-Clad’s D3 Everyday line as the best mix of value and performance for home cooks. The “3” refers to these pans’ 3-ply construction, which features an aluminum core sandwiched between two layers of stainless-steel cladding. That aluminum allows the pan to conduct heat quickly and evenly, and it makes the pan more lightweight than solid stainless-steel cookware. In our testing, we found that those promises held true, and that the D3 pans were easy to clean (just hand-wash with a little soapy water, plus some Bar Keepers Friend if you need a hand getting any remaining bits off) and have continued to perform well over the many years we’ve been using them.

Read more about our favorite stainless steel pans.

D3 3-Ply Stainless-Steel 7-Piece Cookware Set

Includes: 10" fry pan, 3-qt. saucepan with lid, 3-qt. sauté pan with lid, 8-qt. stockpot with lidInduction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: NoMetal-utensil-safe: YesOven-safe: Up to 600°FWarranty: Limited lifetime

Our top pick: While we recommend building your lineup of cookware piece-by-piece over time, a preassembled set is a good, fast solution if you’re looking to replace your arsenal of Teflon. This 7-piece collection of top-performing D3 stainless-steel cookware from All-Clad has everything you need and nothing you don’t, making it the best option for most people. Tight on space? This 5-piece version is a great choice too.

Read more about our favorite cookware sets.

Available sizes: 10.5" (4.5 lb.), 12" (6 lb.), 13.5" (7.5 lb.)Induction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: NoMetal-utensil-safe: YesOven-safe up to: UnknownWarranty: Limited lifetime

About cast iron: If you’re willing to put just a bit of work into caring for your cookware, a cast-iron skillet will easily fill the nonstick pan-size hole in your kitchen. Cast-iron cookware will never quite reach the level of nonstick that a Teflon-coated piece offers, but in our testing, we’ve found that a properly seasoned cast-iron pan is on par with ceramic nonstick—plus it only gets more slick over time as you continue to use it.

Our top pick: After testing more than 20 cast-iron skillets over several years, our current top pick is the Lancaster No. 8 because it’s lightweight, it has a smooth pre-seasoned surface that’s nice and slick right out of the box, and it provides even heat distribution. The one downside is that it’s quite pricey compared to something like Lodge’s iconic cast iron, which we recommend as a great budget alternative. The Lodge is probably the pan most people think of when they hear “cast-iron skillet,” and at around $20, depending on where and when you buy it, it’s one of the best values in the cookware world—particularly because you can keep it forever rather than replacing it every few years. In our testing, it performed just as well as many more expensive pans.

Read more about our favorite cast-iron pans.

Available sizes: .425-qt., .85-qt., 1.25-qt., 1.75-qt., 2.75 qt., 4-qt., 5.5-qt., 7-qt., 8.75-qt., 13.25-qt.Induction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: NoMetal-utensil-safe: NoOven-safe: Up to 500ºFWarranty: Limited lifetime

About enameled cast iron: You may have also heard of enameled cast iron, which is frequently seen in products like our favorite Le Creuset and Staub Dutch ovens. Many people expect enameled cast-iron pots and pans to be nonstick because the ones with light-colored interiors sort of resemble the kinds of ceramic nonstick coatings we wrote about above, but in reality, that’s not the case. That doesn’t mean you can’t cook food in these things without it sticking, but you’ll need to use sufficient fat and heat to make that happen, as you do with a stainless-steel pan. The benefit of enameled cast iron is that it provides superior heat retention and distribution, and protects the cast-iron core from rust and acidity. It's become one of my favorite types of cookware to use at home over the past few years.

Our top pick: The Staub Round Cocotte is my personal top pick when it comes to Dutch ovens, and tied with the Le Creuset in our official product testing. I prefer the Staub’s dark textured enamel interior, which is less prone to showing discoloration. In addition to the round cocotte, I also own the braiser and a deep skillet, both of which I find myself pulling out constantly.

Read more about our favorite Dutch ovens.

Available sizes: 8", 10.25", 11", 12.5"Induction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: NoMetal-utensil-safe: YesOven-safe: Up to 500ºFWarranty: Limited lifetime

About carbon steel: Carbon steel is sort of the Goldilocks cookware because it affords you the nonstick qualities and lightweight feel of a coated nonstick pan and the durability of a cast-iron or stainless-steel skillet. The one caveat is that in order to achieve those nonstick qualities, you’ll need to spend some time properly seasoning your new pan, just as you would with cast iron. But with a bit of work at the outset and occasional maintenance, you’ll be rewarded with an heirloom-worthy piece of cookware that has a well-earned nonstick patina.

Our top pick: De Buyer is one of those famed, old European cookware brands that lots of American home cooks may not be that familiar with. Its “blue” frying pan comes pre-seasoned and will just get better and better as the seasoning improves. As senior writer Wilder Davies notes, you can take specific steps to season it—use a thin layer of oil (as thin as you can possibly get) and put it in a hot oven for an hour—but you can also just keep cooking with it and that seasoning will develop on its own. Another nice feature of this pan in particular, and one that has nothing to do with its seasoning, is its welded-on handle. That means there are no rivets to clean around when you’re done.

Read more about our favorite carbon steel pans.

What types of kitchen gear is PTFE found in?

A skillet may be the first thing you think of when you think of nonstick cookware, but PTFE coatings show up in a host of other items in the kitchen and beyond. On top of skillets, pots, saucepans, and Dutch ovens, you'll also find PTFE in rice cookers, waffle irons, baking sheets, and grill baskets.

You may recognize ceramic nonstick as the material of choice of many of the aesthetically-pleasing, Instagram-viral cookware companies that started popping up in the late 2010s (I’m looking at you, Our Place and Caraway). Ceramic nonstick pans are made without any PFAS. Instead, a gel made from silica is applied and then dried onto the cookware’s metal body to create a nonstick surface.

Sounds great, right? Well, there are a few caveats, the main one being that ceramic nonstick coatings are not built to last. That means you’ll want to be sure to avoid using metal utensils when cooking with them, opting instead for wood or silicone. You’ll also want to avoid exposing them to extremely high temperatures: Even though ceramic cookware is technically more heat tolerant than cookware made with PTFE, high heat will wear down the pan’s ceramic coating. Many manufacturers claim their pans are oven-safe up to certain (often high) temperatures, but we’d recommend using one of our other recommendations above for any stove-to-oven cooking, as those trips to the oven will only further degrade that ceramic coating over time. Similarly, despite any of being dishwasher-safe, hand-washing your pans will prolong their lifespans.

Even if you treat your ceramic nonstick cookware with the utmost care and attention, you still shouldn’t expect it to last you more than one to three years before it starts to lose its nonstick properties. That’s why the best nontoxic nonstick cookware is not necessarily a coated piece of PFOA- or PFAS-free gear—in fact, we’d argue the best nontoxic “nonstick” pans money can buy are made of cast iron, or carbon steel. While these materials are not actually manufactured or marketed as nonstick, each has nonstick properties that can be achieved with proper use and care. .

The bottom line here is that no one needs a coated pan in their life. There is no recipe on this website (or in this world) that requires you to use one, and we tend to think you’re better off investing some time in learning to cook with a more durable type of cookware than spending you money on a full nonstick cookware set. That said, we’re recommending a range of cookware options here for those who are looking for alternatives to traditional PTFE-base nonstick, including a ceramic option for people who aren’t quite ready to kiss coated nonstick goodbye.

#6436. The 2026 Best New Bakeries in America

Precision pastries are sweeping the nation. These bakers are leading the charge.

If there’s one thing we’ve noticed over the past several years, it’s how much bakeries have stepped up their game.

Some embody a personal expression of a baker’s identity, while others push the envelope beyond expected flavor combinations; all excel at a time when “little treat” culture is at its peak. — Missy Frederick, editorial director

Learn more about this year’s Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, and how editors selected them, here.

If one new place in Chicago needs no further hype, it is Bad Butter. You’ll know you’re there when you spot the line cascading out of the whitewashed storefront along West Cortland Street, a queue that doesn’t let up until the pastry case is empty. Formerly a head baker at Soho House Chicago, Dan Koester was stuck at home like the rest of us in 2020, handing off excess home-baked sourdough loaves to friends and family and making some available for free pickup. After he was officially laid off that summer, he launched his own online bakery business, earning a massive following along the way.

One residency at the Emily Hotel later, Koester debuted his Bucktown bakery, demonstrating the full range of his skill. Still warm, charred, and dimpled flats of focaccia showered with scallion furikake rest on its shelves. Impossibly crisp and exquisitely laminated twice-baked almond croissants burst with subtle, aromatic almond paste. A spicy harissa monkey bread with a cloudlike texture is cooled by a pool of creamy labneh drizzled with silky olive oil.

The bakery’s menu has breadth and also manages to arc with the season. Customers snake along the floor waiting their turn to claim a towering cruffin, dusted in fine grains of sugar and piped full of ginger plum jam, or a seasonal tart piled with plump, lacquered blueberries. A pastry box filled with these confections is well worth the wait. — Brenna Houck, dining editorial manager

Born as an underground dinner party operated out of Karla Subero Pittol’s Echo Park garage, Chainsaw finally got its own digs in November 2025 in the form of a lively cafe in Melrose Hill, an unquestionably gentrifying neighborhood that has become home to some of Los Angeles’s best independent restaurants. At the cafe, Subero Pittol channels her Venezuelan heritage through a menu of arepas plump with beans, limey guasacaca, and cheese; a Venezuelan hot dog (“perro caliente”) buoyed by an acidic slaw; and her bracingly tart passionfruit-lime icebox pie, which commands a cult following all its own.

Stepping into Chainsaw feels like you could be in Subero Pittol’s own kitchen as she greets regulars and newcomers as if they are old friends. Customers study a handwritten menu that changes daily — it doesn’t help to come in too attached to any one dish (save the ever-present icebox pie) when you may get tempted by another. The cafe’s impact on Los Angeles feels clear in the near-constant crowds that hover outside, reading their newspapers over an espresso or tucking into the latest of Subero Pittol’s ideas, such as a full English breakfast served for a single day. In a city lacking in untamed Venezuelan cooking, Chainsaw offers a home for Subero Pittol to celebrate the cuisine in a way that feels distinctly Los Angeles. — Rebecca Roland, deputy editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest

With both Afghan and Latin American influences, Diljān gives New Yorkers a bakery with a point of view and innumerable reasons to become a regular. Ali Zaman and Mohamed Ghiasi, owners of Astoria’s Little Flower Cafe, teamed up with Bryan Ford, Honduran American baker and cookbook author, to conceptualize the bakery, now perched on a corner near Atlantic Avenue in Brooklyn Heights.

Their combined talent makes for some of the city’s most compelling baked goods. For the Saffron Shah, laminated pastry holds delicate saffron cream in the shape of a crescent, an important Islamic symbol. Halwa tops the sticky bun, while a swirl of samosa pastry wraps halal lamb under a dusting of powdered sugar. Don’t miss the enormous Afghan flatbread crowned by toppings such as halal beef bacon with scallions or sour cherry cream cheese. The team has also branched into pizzas topped with cheese and Afghan cumin, kofta kebabs, or beef pepperoni. Look for specials like the flan with cardamom-poached apricots and conchas stuffed with firni, a rice pudding. — Nadia Chaudhury, deputy editor, Eater New York

San Francisco’s pastry game is stronger and more competitive than ever before, and Parachute Bakery steps to the forefront of a crowded field with a mix of patisserie standards and seasonal standouts. At his Ferry Building bakery, pastry chef Nasir Armar marries his fine dining training, honed at Michelin-starred Sorrel and Saison, with flavors that make everyone sit up and take notice (and snap a food photo or two for their socials).

Vegetables and savory complements are given their own footing on the menu. Stalks of grilled asparagus shine in a baton-shaped croissant shell, with fennel jam, sheep’s milk ricotta, and ramp pesto alongside them; one brief, bordering-on-gimmicky croissant got piped with clam chowder, a reference to the soup in a bread bowl famously served on the city’s wharf. Even potato-laden samosas and bright tomato shakshuka get interpreted into pastry form. Parachute succeeds with its experimental vision, a hype well-earned that leaves fans clamoring for what they’ll come up with next. — Dianne de Guzman, editor, Eater SF

#6435. This $10,000-a-Pound Spice Could Help Save Colorado Farmers

Beneath Denver’s solar panels, a spice nicknamed “red gold” is yielding a promising harvest that could help Colorado farmers earn more with less water.

At Colorado State University Spur, horticulture graduate student Reece Bailey is investigating whether saffron could become a profitable addition to the state’s farms. His experiments in the campus’s urban gardens and green roof research areas are testing how the crop handles Colorado’s climate, how much water it needs, and whether growing it beneath solar panels improves production.

The appeal starts with its extraordinary value. A pound of saffron typically costs between $600 and $5,000, with some varieties reaching $10,000. Vanilla, the second most expensive spice, sells for roughly $90 to $225 a pound. Those prices caught Bailey’s attention, but the research must establish whether the potential earnings justify the work.

Colorado may seem an unlikely home for a spice closely associated with the Middle East. Yet Iran, which produces roughly 85% of the world’s saffron, has mountainous, semiarid conditions that resemble parts of the state. Bailey sees that overlap as a reason to investigate whether “red gold” could find a foothold on Colorado’s high plains.

The crop also offers an unusual combination of low water demand and late production. Saffron typically blooms in November, potentially bringing farmers income after other harvests have ended. Under suitable conditions, Bailey said, it could provide that additional crop without requiring extra irrigation.

“One thing that’s always been interesting to me is new ideas and novel ways of integrating crops into our environments,” said Bailey, who grew up in Aurora and has worked on Spur’s green roof for three years.

The world’s most expensive spice comes from a remarkably small harvest: the three slender red stigmas inside each purple saffron flower. Collecting enough to produce a pound of dried spice requires roughly 75,000 flowers.

That harvest is painstaking. Flowers open for only a few hours each morning, and workers carefully extract the stigmas, often with tweezers. The amount of hand labor helps explain both saffron’s price and the challenge of turning it into a profitable crop.

“It’s certainly not the easiest crop to grow or the easiest crop to work with, but the investment can be well worth it,” Bailey said.

The Colorado Department of Agriculture has committed $80,000 through its Specialty Crop Block Grant Program to investigate that possibility, particularly as a source of supplemental income late in the season and during dry years.

“For a lot of farmers, the price for their goods isn’t keeping up with the price of inputs, so what we’re really trying to do is find new crops that will work with Colorado’s climate and for our producers’ bottom line,” said Sam Hahn, the department’s next generation and specialty crops program manager. “Saffron has a high labor input, but it could really be a boon for our farmers.”

Successfully growing the flowers would answer only part of the business question. Farmers would still need to assess startup costs, bulb suppliers, equipment, labor availability, and buyers. A valuable spice does not automatically translate into a profitable harvest.

Its labor demands could nevertheless create another benefit. Hahn said the November bloom might provide agricultural jobs during a period when many farmworkers are typically unemployed, while helping farms adapt to a changing climate.

“It’s so important that we experiment with these high-value crops to see if it can supplement the market in our state and keep us competitive,” Hahn said.

Some of the most promising results are emerging 75 feet (23 meters) above the ground. Bailey’s plots occupy the roofs of two CSU Spur buildings, with Denver’s skyline and the Rocky Mountains in view. One grows among native Colorado plants, including sunflowers. Another sits beneath solar panels in an agrivoltaic system, where the same space supports crops and electricity production.

“I’m always curious about how different plants evolve and how they adapt to green roofs, and lately, I’ve come to realize that saffron is almost the ideal plant for these environments,” said Jennifer Bousselot, Bailey’s faculty adviser and an associate professor of horticulture and landscape architecture at CSU.

Spur’s rooftop gardens have carefully selected soil characteristics and are designed to use water efficiently. Saffron also tolerates some shade, and Bailey’s research so far has found that yields nearly double beneath the partial shade of solar arrays.

“This could provide cash flow value for farmers who want to use solar as an energy source, or who happen to be in an urban agriculture setting,” Bailey said.

Water use offers another reason to keep testing. Bailey said saffron requires roughly half as much water as corn and could potentially survive on rainfall alone, making it an appealing candidate for a region where irrigation water is under pressure.

“This crop is incredibly drought resistant,” Bailey said.

The experiments extend beyond Spur’s rooftops to CSU’s Foothills Campus and Denver Botanic Gardens Chatfield Farms, at the base of the mountains south of Denver. At Chatfield Farms, Lauren Hazlett, one of the head growers working at the solar array, has welcomed the sight of flowers appearing as other plants fade.

“I never thought I’d ever be able to see saffron growing, especially in Colorado—it’s something I always associated with the other side of the world,” she said.

Bousselot and Bailey have also sent bulbs to farmers in Paonia, Pueblo, and Montrose. Their reports will help show how saffron performs in working farm operations and whether its potential benefits carry beyond the research plots.

There is already a long history of finding uses for the spice. Alexander the Great, king of the ancient Greek kingdom of Macedon, reportedly bathed in saffron to help heal battle wounds. Doctors once prescribed it for bubonic plague, and Cleopatra used its fragrance to attract potential suitors. Today, it flavors dishes such as paella and risotto and is increasingly sought after in perfumes.

Modern research is also exploring its medicinal properties. Some studies suggest saffron may support mental health and help alleviate depression, while others have investigated its possible anti-inflammatory effects. Those research areas could add to its commercial appeal, although Colorado’s trials are focused on whether farmers can grow and sell it successfully.

“Up until now, we haven’t really been able to study saffron in Colorado at a deeper level, but the demand is there, and I only think we’ll be talking about it more and more,” Bailey said.

#6434. Shape-Shifting Robotic "Slugs" Could One Day Crawl Across Alien Worlds

Robots have been a mainstay of our early space exploration efforts. But they normally have wheels. Or in some cases, rotors. While those solutions are great on flat ground, they struggle with jagged boulders or tight crevices. So engineers have been working on alternative robotic form factors, and a recent paper in Nature Machine Intelligence from researchers at Colorado State Universityâs Adaptive Robotics Lab, describes a unique morphology using a design principle typically seen in architecture rather than robotics - tensegrity.

Tensegrity was originally made popular by Buckminster Fuller in the mid-20th century. Itâs a blend of the words âtensionâ and âintegrityâ, and at its core it uses rigid rods that push outwards against elastic cables that pull inwards. So, instead of relying on heavy metal hinges, the rods âfloatâ on a web of tension.

This isnât the first time the idea has been brought to space exploration, though. NASA has been exploring its use cases for over a decade, perhaps most notably with the SUPERball - a spherical cage designed to withstand high-speed planetary landings without parachutes by absorbing the shocks of impact across its network of cables.

Fraser talks about some other robots that could end up exploring other worlds.

But this is one of the first times the idea has been applied to robotics. The CSU researchers have developed what they call the Tensegrity-based Continuum Robot (TeCoBot). Measuring in at around 587 mm (~2 ft) long and weighing around 600 grams, the cylindrical bot combined a squishy, flexible spine with adaptable dual mechanical claws, which provide the real interesting use cases of the technology.

TeCoBotâs body is made out of four stacked icosahedral tensegrity modules that create a continuous, flexible backbone. Each module is built around six lightweight rods suspended inside a 3D printed stretchy lattice. Three cables made up of 40-lb braided fishing wire run through the center of the robot, and by pulling on each of them with small motors attached to its base, the robot can bend in any direction - like an âelephantâs trunkâ as a press release puts it. It can also scrunch down to around half its original size if all three lines are pulled at the same time.

But whatâs most interesting about the technology is its modularity, which relies on the claws on either end. These claws are swappable, so if a robot needs to handle delicate cargo engineers can put a soft-padded claw on it. But, if needed, those soft pads can be swapped out for a heavier duty gripper claw that uses a worm gear to clamp and hold onto another gripper without draining any battery.

Fraser talks about the concept of "grey goo" - or self-replicating robots able to automate space exploration.

This unlocks all sorts of additional opportunities. As a stand-alone single robot, TeCoBot is already relatively capable - it can inch along like a caterpillar, roll sideways, and even climb vertically. It also exhibits what roboticists call âembodied intelligenceâ that means its body can naturally give way when bumped or when it runs into something without needing a whole control system to adjust to the changed environment.

But when they combine together, they unlock whole new operating modes. Using their claws to grab one another, three TeCoBots can self-configure into a wide variety of shapes. The paper discusses three robots wrapping themselves around a large pipe, and forming a H-shaped walker to crawl through tight spaces. But perhaps most interestingly for anyone who hates cleaning as much as this author, they are also capable of teaming up to clean off a table.

Those feats might not seem immediately applicable to space exploration, but the underlying modularity and adaptability would be extremely useful in the rough craters of the Moon or underground caverns on Mars. Weâve already reported on a snake robot designed to explore those exact locations, and this seems like a step up in functionality from that.

Video of the TeCoBot in action. Credit - Adaptive Robotics Lab YouTube Channel

That being said, it still has a long way to go before weâd see it on another heavenly body. Currently, engineers have to manually control the bots via a WiFi connection - which isnât exactly easy on deep space missions. But they do plan to make improvements on the design, upgrading the motors for faster movement and adding swarm intelligence to allow dozens of these modular robots to band together. If that development goes as planned, these elephant trunk styled robots might serve as some of our most intrepid deep space explorers.

CSU / EurekAlert - Inspired by elephant trunks, these shape-shifting robots bend, grab and team up

In a key coastal area of Peru, violence was low despite the practice of human sacrifice.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Despite engaging in human sacrifice, the people who lived in the Lambayeque Valley of northern Peru had low levels of violence, a new study of their remains finds.

Human sacrifice occurred in the valley over the millennia. It's thought that at least some of these mass sacrifices were attempts to appease the gods in the wake of El Niño, a periodic weather phenomenon that can lead to intense rains and flooding in Peru and droughts in other parts of South and Central America.

"We have one example at the site of Sicán where around [A.D.] 1050/1100, around 200 individuals were killed and ritualistically buried during an intense El Niño event," study co-author Haagen Klaus, an anthropology professor at George Mason University in Virginia, told Live Science in an email.

Other human sacrifice findings include more than 200 children found near the modern-day town of Huanchaco who were sacrificed sometime between 600 and 800 years ago, possibly during an El Niño.

However, despite the occurrence of human sacrifice, levels of violence unrelated to sacrifice were actually quite low in the Lambayeque Valley. In the study, scientists analyzed the skeletal remains of 1,519 people from the Lambayeque Valley who lived between roughly 1500 B.C. and A.D. 1800, and whose remains were preserved enough to detect signs of violent trauma, including interpersonal violence.

A skull showing blunt force trauma that dates to the Chimu period, roughly 1375 to 1490.

Of these skeletons, "only 25 (1.6%) exhibited traumatic lesions consistent with interpersonal conflict, and 77 exhibited post-cranial traumatic lesions consistent with accidental trauma (5.1%)," Klaus and co-author Thomas Snyder, a bioarchaeologist at New York University, wrote in the paper, which was published Nov. 8 in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology.

The team didn't find any link between a person's sex and violence, they noted. The findings mean that despite the presence of human sacrifice, the amount of violence unrelated to sacrifice was low. This leaves a question: Why?

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

A healed fracture on the left leg of a person who lived sometime between 1000 to 650 B.C. The fracture may have been from an accident.

"Ritual violence may have alleviated non-ritual violence by creating spaces where social tensions could get worked out in a few different ways," Klaus said.

It's important to remember that other areas of Peru also practiced human sacrifice but didn't have the same low levels of interpersonal violence. Klaus noted that areas in the Peruvian highlands sometimes had higher rates of interpersonal violence. In their paper, Klaus and Snyder noted that societies that originated in the highlands, such as the Tiwanaku, Wari and Inca had to grapple with poorer soils and cold temperatures, and these challenges may have been a factor in increasing the levels of interpersonal violence.

The "evidence of sub-lethal and lethal violence forceful enough to break bone is significantly higher in some areas of Peru's highlands," Klaus said. He and Snyder noted in their paper that the inhabitants of the Lambayeque Valley may have had better access to marine and water resources, such as seafood and rivers that could be used for agricultural irrigation, than those who lived in highland areas. Access to these resources may have helped alleviate interpersonal violence in the valley by providing more food resources, they wrote.

Aside from practicing human sacrifice, people in the valley may have engaged in other practices that helped lower levels of interpersonal violence, researchers who were not involved in the new study told Live Science.

Environmental conditions may have helped reduce conflict or there could be "really unusual cultural practices in this region of avoiding or mediating conflict — both between and within groups," Elizabeth Arkush, an anthropology professor at the University of Pittsburgh, said in an email.

Constanza Ceruti, an anthropologist and explorer with the National Geographic Society, said in an email that she's glad that researchers are studying human sacrifices "after decades of being ignored as a taboo topic in academic discussion." She praised the study’s large sample size and noted that human sacrifice is a "phenomenon primarily associated [with] the manipulation and concentration of power by elites."

Jordi Rivera Prince, an anthropology professor at Tulane University, said that the findings dovetail with her excavations in the region, where she has "found little evidence of violent trauma during the Salinar (400-200 BCE), a period of great social change in the Andes."

Weston McCool, an archaeology professor at Cal Poly, said in an email that the newly published paper "is an interesting study that provides additional evidence for a sharp break in patterns of violence between the Andean coast and highlands." He noted that it "supports the hypothesis that coastal populations were buffered from terrestrial environmental downturns in ways that highland populations were not. The nature of that resilience, however, remains an important question for future research."

Snyder, T. J., & Klaus, H. D. (2026). Pax Lambayeque? Trauma, interpersonal violence, and environment over 3,000 years in the Lambayeque Valley Complex, Peru. Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, 5, 1889466. https://doi.org/10.3389/fearc.2026.1889466

He has also written for The Independent (UK), The Canadian Press (CP) and The Associated Press (AP), among others. Owen has a bachelor of arts degree from the University of Toronto and a journalism degree from Ryerson University.

#6432. What You Need to Know About Japanese Knives

The popularity of Japanese knives in home and commercial kitchens has exploded in the last few years, and for good reason: A lot of them outperform their Western counterparts in kitchen tests. Western-style knives are bulkier, all-purpose kitchen tools—years ago, it would be common for many chefs to use the heavy bolster near the heel of the blade to crack open a can of tomatoes during service. Japanese knives (and Japanese-style knives produced by manufacturers elsewhere) are designed with precision cuts in mind and usually have a specific purpose. However, because they’re designed with that specificity in mind, it can be tricky to know what you need and what you’ll use.

Thankfully, we’ve reviewed a wide variety of Japanese-style knives for Bon Appétit and have assembled a roundup to help you identify exactly what your kitchen needs. While there are more styles of Japanese knives than those listed here, these options have all been thoroughly tested, giving us the confidence to speak to each knife’s utility. Before we jump into specific styles, however, it’s useful to give a quick rundown on some of the broad strokes of what makes a Japanese-style knife unique.

Many Japanese knives are designed for push cuts or pull-through slicing rather than the rocking chop of a heavy Western chef’s knife. They tend to have a straighter edge than their Western counterparts, making them slightly less adept at speeding through a mince of herbs, but more precise in their cuts. Most Japanese-style knives also feature a sheep’s-foot tip that curves down to the point, giving the user more control over fine-point work.

Japanese knives are often made with a harder steel than their Western counterparts. Harder steel helps a knife’s edge retain sharpness, which lets manufacturers use steeper sharpening angles for a finer edge. This helps most Japanese knives slice more delicately than Western knives, though harder steel can chip on material like ice or bone.

Traditional Japanese-style knives are only sharpened on one side, giving them a much finer edge than the 50/50 bevel of Western-style knives that are sharpened on both sides. Some modern Japanese knife makers have pivoted to a 50/50 style bevel for ease of sharpening; however, when you’re shopping, you’ll encounter plenty of knives with 70/30 bevel with the inside edge (the left edge for a right-handed knife) sharpened at a steeper angle. A 70/30 bevel is easier to maintain than a single-bevel but offers a sharper edge than a 50/50 bevel.

Many traditional Japanese kitchen knives feature a wa-style handle—an octagonal wood handle that envelops a hidden knife tang (the metal part of the knife that connects to the handle). Wa-style handles help keep knives lighter and nimbler, while many Western-style knives use full-tang construction, adding weight and heft to the blade. Many modern Japanese knife makers, though, combine full-tang knife handles with Japanese blade shapes to create a hybrid-style knife that’s both durable and adept at slicing.

The gyuto, or Japanese chef’s knife, originated in Japan in the early 1900s, when French cooking began to gain popularity in a rapidly modernizing country. This knife style took cues from the traditional French chef’s knife and combined them with elements of traditional Japanese knife making. The resulting Japanese take on a chef’s knife was primarily designed for slicing meat, though it also features a curved edge that makes it easy to chop herbs. Compared to a Western chef’s knife, the gyuto has a straighter blade and a drop point tip with a lower overall profile. This is primarily designed so that the user can place the knife’s tip on the cutting board and draw it through food, taking advantage of the gyuto’s sharp edge and thin blade for precision slicing. But while the gyuto excels at slicing meat, its general shape makes it an overall great pick to anchor your knife collection, and many home cooks opt for a gyuto as their daily driver over a traditional chef’s knife.

We’ve long been fans of the gyuto fan here at Bon Appétit, with MAC’s Professional Hollow Ground Chef’s Knife topping our chef’s knife review for years. For a wicked sharp, more traditional option, we really like the Kazan Arare by Shibata gyuto, which impressed us so much we had to give it its own review.

Increasingly common as a part of brands’ knife sets, the santoku knife is a relatively modern knife shape, first appearing in the 1940s or so. Nicknamed the three virtues knife, the santoku draws on the gyuto, nakiri, and deba to create a well-rounded utility knife that’s great for cutting meat, fish, and vegetables. Typically, these knives feature a pretty steep sheep’s-foot tip for precision point work, a tall heel for push cuts, and just enough curve for pull-through slicing and rock-chopping. A santoku knife is great for well-rounded utility work—think cutting cheese and an apple for a snack, slicing leftover roasted chicken to make a sandwich, or dicing an onion for a curry.

Typically, we like a santoku knife that’s between six and seven inches, so it contrasts with the longer gyuto. Our favorite overall model is the MAC Professional Santoku Knife, but if you’d like a razor-sharp version with a traditional wa-style handle, we love the Kazan Ginsan Nashiji Santoku.

Nakiri knives have a straight edge and a sturdy spine, specifically designed for chopping vegetables. Sometimes referred to as a vegetable cleaver, the nakiri excels at push cuts, making it great for both matchsticking carrots and breaking down tough-skinned squash. Since most gyutos feature thin blades and fine edges, the nakiri also holds a spot in the Japanese knife lineup as a tougher, heavier knife for more demanding tasks. Traditional nakiri knives may also feature a blunt, rounded tip, which can be rotated against the cutting board to create a smooth, chopping motion.

The Tojiro DP Damascus Nakiri is by far our overall favorite tested nakiri knife for its extremely sharp edge and overall balance, but it’s also pricey. We also really like the Tojiro Classic nakiri, though it can have stock issues due to its popularity and price point.

The deba knife is a traditional Japanese knife designed for fish butchery. Unlike a Western fillet knife, which is designed to be flexible and nimble, the deba is a heavy, sturdy blade with a thick spine that gives the heel of the blade a cleaver-like feel. But a deba knife is also designed for precision slicing, and it usually features a traditional single-bevel edge. That single-bevel edge allows the knife to come to a finer point than a double-bevel edge, and the sheep’s-foot tip adds to the deba knife’s ability to portion out delicate fish fillets as well.

We haven’t tested deba knives because they require a bit of knowledge and skill to use them for breaking down whole fish, but if you’re intrigued by the shape and want a cleaver-like knife for your kitchen, the Seki Mago Roku Deba from Kai is an affordable, solid option. Otherwise, we think most people would be better served looking to a nakiri or santoku knife.

Named for the French word petite, which means small, the petty knife is often a replica of the gyuto, just in a much, much smaller form. Most petty knives are around five inches long and feature a thin, lightly curved blade with a drop point tip and heel just tall enough to keep your fingers from bashing into the cutting board. Petty knives are great utility knives for small tasks, like dicing a shallot, slicing garlic, or slicing herbs, but they’re also long and nimble enough to be great slicers. Unless you do a lot of handheld turning and peeling, a petty knife is a great replacement for a paring knife in your lineup.

We found that both the MAC Professional Petty Knife and the Tojiro Classic Petty Knife were sharp enough to slice a steak while still being the perfect size to slice strawberries for your morning yogurt bowl.

Traditionally a fisherman’s knife used for all sorts of purposes on the boat, the funayuki is an old-school knife shape that predates the gyuto and santoku, and it likely helped inspire both shapes. The traditional funayuki is a shorter knife, around seven inches long, with a narrow, pointed tip and a tall heel. They are santoku-sized but gyuto-shaped. Unlike the deba knife, which was a heavy, single-bevel knife used for fish butchery, the funayuki was designed to be light and nimble so that fishermen could fillet their lunch while at sea. These days, most home cooks might pick up a funayuki as a secondary, shorter gyuto, or opt for this shape over a santoku as an all-purpose utility knife with a narrower tip.

Though it’s not as common in modern kitchens, one of our favorite Japanese chef’s knives is the Akiru-Saku Funayuki Gyuto, which is more traditionally shaped like a funayuki but is advertised as a gyuto since the two shapes are so similar.

The kiritsuke is a Japanese slicing knife with an angular “sword tip” that allows the user to make precision cuts. The initial design combined a long slicing shape and tall heel, making the kiritsuke a hybrid knife, similar to the santoku. For most people, the kiritsuke will be a version of an all-purpose chef’s knife that could take the place of a gyuto as a daily driver, with the big difference coming in the shape of the tip.

When reviewing chef’s knives, we found that the Shun Classic Kiritsuke was a great all-purpose chef’s knife with a unique tip that some people might prefer over a gyuto, since it curves upward more like a Western chef’s knife and allows for more of a rock chop motion.

Boning and fillet knives are often unitaskers that don’t see much use unless you’re a fan of home butchery, but the Japanese honesuki is an even more specialized boning knife shape. Designed specifically for poultry, the honesuki is a steep, wedge-shaped knife with a very fine point and a tall heel. The goal is to have a knife that’s delicate enough to slip between a chicken joint while being sturdy enough to cut through cartilage. While the honesuki was designed for a specific purpose, we find that this shape is more versatile and can be swapped in for a petty knife for other small chopping and dicing tasks in ways that a curved fillet knife can’t.

We like the MAC Professional Honesuki as a great option that could tackle most boning-knife tasks while remaining sharp and versatile enough for utility work. If you find yourself breaking down a whole chicken while also wanting a strawberry-slicing knife, the honesuki could be a nonconventional multitasker.

#6431. Scientists Discover a Powerful Plastic-Eating Enzyme Hiding in an Ordinary Compost Heap

An enzyme found in compost broke down small amounts of polyurethane foam in laboratory tests, offering an early lead toward gentler ways to recycle a stubborn plastic.

The polyurethane used in mattress foam, shoe soles, and refrigerator insulation is notoriously difficult to recycle on an industrial scale. A very large share of the millions of metric tons produced worldwide ends up in landfills or incinerators, taking potentially reusable material with it.

Nylon presents a similar challenge. Used in clothing, bags, cars, ropes, engine components, and fishing nets, it is another plastic made from crude oil, a finite resource. Researchers want to break both materials down into their pure components so those ingredients can become new polyurethane and nylon. Chemical and biological approaches are making progress, but the solutions emerging from laboratories are not yet ready for industrial use.

Researchers from Aarhus University and the Danish Technological Institute went looking for help among bacteria. Their search took in a Kenyan landfill, a tropical zoo, the guts of wax moth larvae, and a compost heap near Aarhus. The best candidate came from the compost, where a bacterium produced an enzyme with an ability that could prove useful far beyond the heap.

Researchers collected bacteria from plastic-contaminated environments, including a tropical zoo, a landfill in Kenya, compost and larval guts. Using fluorescent probes and fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS), they isolated bacteria capable of cleaving chemical bonds found in polyurethane and nylon. The active enzymes were then purified and identified using chromatography, activity assays and mass spectrometry. In total, the researchers identified 10 polyurethane-degrading enzymes and 2 nylon-degrading enzymes. Credit: Rosie Graham / Angewandte Chemie

Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions. To find ones that can break down plastic, researchers conventionally search genome databases for gene sequences resembling those of enzymes already known to do the job. That approach has yielded useful enzymes, but there are relatively few known examples to guide the search.

This team used bioprospecting, which means searching nature for organisms and genetic material that could be useful in research or industry. It was the first time researchers had searched on such a large scale and across such varied environments for enzymes capable of degrading polyurethane, also called PUR, and nylon.

The idea came to Andreas Møllebjerg as he prepared to begin a postdoctoral position at what was then the Interdisciplinary Nano Science Center (iNANO) at Aarhus University. He was joining a new project investigating whether natural enzymes could break down plastic. Møllebjerg, a co-author of the resulting study, recently published in Angewandte Chemie, was responsible for collecting bacteria from different environments.

“I suggested looking for suitable enzymes in places where it is warm, because bacteria thrive and grow well there all year round. And preferably somewhere plastic has been present for a long time. A year and a half later, I was on a plane to Kenya, followed by half an hour on the back of a local student’s motorbike on the way to a huge landfill. He helped me collect samples and communicate with the hundreds of people who lived on and off the landfill,” he says.

Møllebjerg and PhD student and co-author Malthe Kjær Bendtsen also traveled 34 kilometers, about 21 miles, to collect plastic waste at Randers Regnskov Tropical Zoo. Møllebjerg bought a bag of wax moth larvae from a pet food shop so the team could investigate enzymes from bacteria in their guts. At a recycling center about 10 kilometers, or 6 miles, from the university, he collected a shovelful of compost.

Those samples gave the researchers millions of bacteria to examine. Finding a useful enzyme required more than showing that a bacterium could react with a convenient laboratory substitute for plastic.

“It was like a three-stage rocket, where we gradually narrowed them down. We started by finding bacteria that could break down the fluorescent model material. Then we isolated the enzymes capable of breaking down exactly that fluorescent material. And finally, we tested the enzymes on increasingly realistic materials,” Bendtsen explains.

This 90-hour time-lapse video shows enzymatic degradation of two different molecules that mimic nylon. The second and fourth vials show CCPUR1 breaking down the two molecules, while the first and third vials show an inactive enzyme. Credit: Samuel Peña Díaz, Aarhus University, and Andreas Sommerfeldt, Danish Technological Institute

For the initial screening, the researchers mixed bacteria with molecules designed to mimic chemical bonds in polyurethane and nylon. The molecules lit up when they encountered a bacterium containing a suitable enzyme. Using fluorescence-activated cell sorting, or FACS, a machine could screen the bacteria and pick out glowing cells at a rate of up to 10,000 per second.

The search identified 29 plastic-degrading bacteria and 12 enzymes with varying abilities to break down polyurethane and nylon. The most promising enzyme was CCPUR1, from the compost bacterium Chelatococcus composti. Its name takes “CC” from the bacterium and “PUR” from PURase, shorthand for polyurethane hydrolase, an enzyme capable of breaking down polyurethane.

Testing on more realistic materials showed both its potential and its limitations. Given polyurethane mattress foam in powdered form, CCPUR1 broke down just under 1% in three days. That leaves a substantial gap between detecting an enzyme’s activity and using it to recycle plastic on an industrial scale.

CCPUR1 nevertheless had several useful characteristics. Its unusually wide binding cleft, a groove where it accommodates the material it acts on, gives large polymer molecules room to fit. Polymers are the long molecules that make up plastics. The enzyme was also particularly stable, withstanding higher temperatures and a range of solvents better than the other candidates.

Its origins in compost offer an explanation for those abilities. Compost contains stubborn plant materials such as wax and lignin, and an enzyme that evolved to break down those substances can also happen to work on plastic. Compost heaps can reach 80°C, or 176°F, so enzymes functioning there need enough stability to withstand the heat.

The team has since worked to improve CCPUR1. In a follow-up study published September 11, 2026, in Chem Catalysis, the researchers collaborated with the University of Porto, using computer simulations and targeted edits to the DNA instructions for making the enzyme.

Within three days, the modified enzyme broke down around 1.4% of the polyurethane in foam from a real shoe sole, without any pretreatment of the plastic. That experiment used a different material from the powdered mattress foam in the original study. Postdoctoral researcher Rosie Graham, who was responsible for testing the enzymes on plastic materials in the laboratory, is the first author of the follow-up study.

The other 11 enzymes could also have a role. They work best on small pieces of plastic and may complement CCPUR1 in future combinations of processes. Because enzymes are selective about what they act on, the researchers envisage using an enzyme cocktail in stages. Polyurethane could first be broken down and washed away, followed by the addition of nylon-degrading enzymes. Chemical methods cannot separate those tasks in the same way.

Making these processes practical may require mechanical and chemical treatments that make the plastic easier for enzymes to attack. Chemical degradation of polyurethane and nylon is itself a major research field, including at Aarhus University. The scale of the remaining challenge is one reason the team compares efficient polyurethane recycling to finding the holy grail.

“But the research highlights the strength of enzymes. Their real advantage when it comes to recycling is that they work under mild conditions, meaning at lower temperatures and pressures than those used in most recycling technologies today,” Graham says.

Reference: “Environmental Identification of Novel Enzymes for Polyurethane and Polyamide Degradation” by Malthe Kjær Bendtsen, Andreas Møllebjerg, Samuel Peña-Díaz, Rosie Graham, Nicolai Claus Petersen, Bjørk Nolsøe Isaksen, Mathias Carstensen, Martin B. Johansen, Andreas Sommerfeldt, Allan R. Petersen, Iddi Khamisi Chuma, Cecilie Ryberg, Thomas Rea Wittenborn, Virginia Gichuru, Huabing Wang, Carsten Scavenius, Alexander Sandahl and Daniel E. Otzen, 26 June 2026, Angewandte Chemie International Edition. DOI: 10.1002/anie.6159643

This work is supported by the Novo Nordisk Foundation through the Challenge Grant NNF22OC0072891 to the Center EnZync.

#6430. Dense Galaxy Clusters Foster Mechanisms That Throttle Star Formation

Star-forming regions are plentiful in the Milky Way, and they're some of the most visually glorious sights in the galaxy. In these regions, the powerful light from massive young stars shapes and energizes gas into glowing arrangements of filaments and billowing clouds. Astronomers study these intently, and astrophotographers share their enthusiasm.

One of the most well-known star forming regions is the stunning Orion Nebula, captured in all its glory by space telescopes like the Hubble and the JWST, and by astrophotographers on the ground. Most of us have seen some of these images, even if only in passing.

Despite the presence of so many star-forming regions, the Milky Way only forms about 6 or 7 new stars every year. This pales in comparison with the cosmos' peak star formation rate about 10 billion years ago. That period of time is called the Cosmic Noon, and during that epoch, star formation was as much as 30 times greater than it is today, all across the Universe, including in the Milky Way.

The star formation rate has slowed precipitously, and today it's dropped by about 97%. What caused this drop in star formation? Stars form from cold, dense gas, so something must have happened to the gas.

Astronomers know that environmental effects play a leading role in diminishing gas supplies and slowing star formation, both inside galaxies and between galaxies in galaxy groups. Stellar winds can blow gas away, and astrophysical jets from active galactic nuclei (AGN) can heat gas and disperse it. There are other types of disruptions, like gas stripping via galaxy mergers, and galaxy deformations from the same mergers. Sometimes galaxies can merge and gas can be spread out into space in tidal tails. In other cases, galactic star-forming gas is heated through interactions with the much hotter intergalactic medium, or even stripped away by these encounters.

Since most galaxies exist in galaxy groups, researchers try to understand the drop in star formation in these environments. But measurements of the gas supply in galaxy groups are rare.

New research to be published in Astronomy and Astrophysics measured how the supply of molecular gas, the raw material of star formation, is shaped by a galaxy's wider environment in dense galaxy clusters. It's titled "Probing the molecular gas content of galaxies in an over-dense group at z~0.7: A test case for environmental quenching," and the lead author is Jonathan Freundlich. Freundlich is an astrophysicist at the University of Strasbourg, Astronomical Observatory (ObAS). The work is focused on a distant galaxy group called COSMOS-Gr30.

This image shows a dense region of the COSMOS-Gr30 galaxy group about 6.5 billion light-years away from Earth. The observations were made using the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope. The image was the ESO's Picture of the Week on the 13th of November 2017. Image Credit: ESO/T. Contini (IRAP, Toulouse), B. Epinat (LAM, Marseille)

When astronomers want to probe molecular hydrogen (H2), the raw stuff of star formation, they face an obstacle. Despite being by far the most abundant molecule in the interstellar medium and the primary ingredient in the giant molecular clouds (GMCs) where stars form, H2 is virtually undetectable in radio observations. Since star formation needs cold gas, radio is the way to observe it. Astronomers make us of the fact that carbon monoxide (CO) is the second most abundant component of GMCs, and observe it as a proxy for H2. In particular, they measure what are called CO(2-1) emissions, which appear when CO drops its energy state and releases a photon with radio levels of energy. Then they rely on a standard conversion factor between H2 and CO to turn CO observations into H2 observations.

That's what they did in this research that focuses on COSMOS-Gr30, an exceptionally dense group of galaxies.

"We investigated the impact of group environment on molecular gas reservoirs at an intermediate redshift by observing the CO(2-1) emission from the galaxy group COSMOS-Gr30 at zâ¼0.7 with the Institut de Radioastronomie Millimetrique (IRAM) NOrthern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA) and 30m telescope," the authors write. This is a very dense environment where massive cosmic filaments intersect and host a large structure of ionized gas that's about 100 billion square light years in size.

This is the COSMOS-Gr30 galaxy group, located about 7 billion light years away, as seen with the JWST. The contours show the structure of diffuse ionized gas in between the group's member galaxies, as observed with the Multi-Unit Spectral Explorer instrument on the ESO's Very Large Telescope. Image Credits: Casey et al. 2023, Epinat et al. 2018, 2024, Freundlich et al. 2026.

The researchers measured the gas in the interstellar medium (ISM) inside of the galaxies as well as the gas in the intergalactic medium (IGM) between the galaxies. These simultaneous measurements generated a more comprehensive look at star-forming gas and its availability in dense galaxy cluster environments. It revealed mechanisms responsible for quenching star formation in dense clusters.

"Deep MUSE (Multi-Unit Spectroscopic Explorer) observations reveal a large, massive structure of ionized gas surrounding eight galaxies of the group, including one active galactic nucleus (AGN) host," the authors write. "This gas is not pristine and was likely expelled from the galaxies through both internal processes, such as star formation and AGN outflows, and external processes in the dense environment, such as ram pressure stripping and tidal interactions."

The results also show that less than one-third of the gas displaced from COSMOS-Gr30's member galaxies and moved into the diffuse structure is cold enough to form stars.

The researchers found that galaxies in this dense environment have only about 20% to 40% of the molecular gas found in typical main-sequence galaxies. Main-sequence galaxies are benchmark galaxies that form stars at a steady, typical rate.

Astronomers have studied molecular gas and its availability for star formation inside galaxies before, and they've done it for the intergalactic medium, too. But this work takes it a step further by characterizing gas availability in dense cluster environments. The research "... highlights the importance of simultaneously probing gas reservoirs within galaxies and the surrounding intragroup medium to capture environmental quenching in action," the authors explain.

"In the case of CGr30, the depletion of molecular gas within galaxies, combined with the presence of an extended gas structure, provides a consistent picture of environmental quenching," the researchers write.

This is the Northern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA) radio interferometer, located in the Hautes-Alpes at an altitude of 2550m. It has 12x15m radio dishes, and was used in this work to observe CO emissions in the galaxies of the COSMOS-Gr30 group. Image Credit: IRAM-gre via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

They do state a caveat with their results, and that regards some of the uncertainties in their work, including the star-formation rate (SFR) and how accurate the CO observations are as a proxy for molecular hydrogen.

"Although the uncertainties are significant, this suggests that environmental processes efficiently deplete molecular gas reservoirs in the galaxies of this group," the authors write.

More observations of COSMOS-Gr30 will address these uncertainties, and ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, will provide important observations. It's the most powerful radio antenna array in the world, more powerful than NOEMA used in this work. It has 66 high-precision 12 meter antennas that can collectively create a baseline up to 16 km wide. It can zoom into regions like COSMOS-Gr30 to uncover unseen detail.

"Furthermore, more precise SFR measurements are necessary to decrease the uncertainties, and larger samples of target galaxies in groups will allow us to assess group-to-group variance," the authors conclude.

Evan Gough is a science-loving guy with no formal education who loves Earth, forests, hiking, and heavy music. He's guided by Carl Sagan's quote: "Understanding is a kind of ecstasy."
