#6373. Scientists Crack a Decades-Old Mystery That Could Unlock Faster Internet

By untangling how the crystal barium titanate interacts with light, researchers have supplied data that could reduce costly trial and error in designing faster optical communication devices.

When light carries data through a communication device, absorption by the materials inside can weaken the signal. Engineers trying to build faster, more efficient devices need to predict how light will travel through those materials and how much will be lost before they commit to a design.

For a promising material called barium titanate, or BTO, those measurements have varied widely for decades. A KAIST-led research team has now clarified how it interacts with light, providing data that could help engineers design devices more reliably and reduce costly rounds of fabrication and redesign.

BTO offers a useful way to control light because applying an electric field changes its refractive index, a measure of how much light slows as it passes through a material. Its strong response to an electric field, known as the Pockels effect, makes it promising for optical modulators. These devices use electrical signals to control light and encode information onto it.

The difficulty is that a BTO crystal can contain small regions, called domains, with different crystal orientations. Those regions can interact with light differently, so measuring them together blends their responses. That makes it harder to determine the material’s underlying optical properties and predict how it will behave in a device.

To reduce that mixing, the team led by Professor Min Seok Jang of KAIST’s School of Electrical Engineering examined two types of single-crystal BTO samples with relatively uniform domain orientations. The researchers used Mueller-matrix spectroscopic ellipsometry, a technique that measures changes in light’s polarization, or the orientation of its electric-field vibrations, when it reflects from or passes through a material. Those changes provide information about how the material affects light.

Their analysis covered wavelengths from 190 nanometers (nm) to 40 micrometers (μm), spanning the ultraviolet to the far-infrared. Because BTO interacts with light differently across that range, the researchers divided it into three spectral regions and used an analytical approach suited to each. They determined how the refractive index and absorption properties vary with both wavelength and crystal orientation.

The team also developed a method for calculating the overall optical response of a crystal containing differently oriented domains. Using the orientations and relative proportions of those domains, the method accounts for the mixed internal structure that had made BTO’s properties difficult to establish.

Even in the wavelength range where BTO is nearly transparent, the researchers were able to quantify very weak absorption. They combined ellipsometry with separate transmittance measurements, which record how much light passes through a sample, to determine extinction coefficients as low as approximately 10⁻⁵ in the 2–10 μm range. The extinction coefficient describes how strongly a material absorbs light, with smaller values indicating weaker absorption.

Together, these measurements help answer two practical questions about a waveguide, a structure that guides light through a device. The refractive index helps designers predict how the light will travel, while the extinction coefficient helps them estimate how much will be lost to absorption. Engineers can use the data to assess devices of different sizes and shapes before fabrication. Potential applications include communications modulators, devices that generate light at new wavelengths, and circuits that process quantum information using light.

KAIST, led by President Choongsik Bae, announced the work on November 8. The study was conducted in collaboration with Professor Harry A. Atwater’s team at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), the Korea Research Institute of Standards and Science (KRISS), and U.S.-based J.A. Woollam Co.

“This study reveals the optical response of barium titanate, which had long remained unclear, and provides a reliable reference for how the material interacts with light,” said Professor Min Seok Jang. He added that the findings are expected to contribute to optical communication devices that reduce light loss and enable faster data transmission, as well as quantum photonic devices that require precise control of light.

Reference: “Broadband Optical Characterization of Tetragonal Barium Titanate by Mueller-Matrix Spectroscopic Ellipsometry” by Jiwon Kang, Nina Hong, Christopher M. Yi, Yun Su Go, Martin Thomaschewski, Hwi Je Woo, Prachi Thureja, Junghoon Jahng, Harry A. Atwater and Min Seok Jang, 20 October 2026, ACS Photonics. DOI: 10.1021/acsphotonics.6c01514

This research was supported by the Culture, Sports and Tourism R&D Program through the Korea Creative Content Agency (KOCCA), with funding from the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism; the Basic Science Research Program through the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF), with funding from the Ministry of Education; the Ministry of Science and ICT; and the U.S. Air Force Office of Scientific Research (AFOSR).

#6372. A high-fiber diet may clear away plastic in the gut

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Mice that ate lots of fiber had far less particles accumulate in the body

A diet that includes high-fiber foods, like these vegetables, might come with a surprise benefit. Fiber could help carry nanoplastics out of the body, suggests a new study in mice.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Here’s a new reason to eat your beans and greens.

A high-fiber diet may help sweep plastic particles from the gut, researchers report October 15 in Nature Communications. In mice that ingested plastic, eating loads of fiber daily kept the particles from piling up in the intestines. The finding hints at fiber’s power to protect the body from environmental garbage, says Eddy Y. Zeng, an environmental scientist at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have long known that fiber can improve our health, in part by lowering cholesterol, keeping blood sugar levels in check and easing food through the gut. But now, Zeng says, his team’s results suggest an additional benefit.

We live in a world littered with plastic, much of it too small to see. These micro and nanoplastics, shed by disposable water bottles, fast food containers and other worldly junk, can make their way into our bodies. It’s not completely clear what such shards do to our health, but we have some hints. Scientists have linked plastic particles in people’s arteries to increased risk of heart attack and stroke. And mice that ingest tiny bits of plastic can show signs of organ injury.

Zeng’s team thought dietary fiber might provide some defense. Fiber forms a complex network of polymers that could trap ingested plastics like flies in a spider web, he says.

The researchers put mice on low-, medium-, or high-fiber diets, then fed them plastic particles. Over the next 24 hours, the medium- and high-fiber groups of mice cleared more particles from their bodies than their low-fiber counterparts, the team discovered. That’s important, Zeng says, because these particles can do damage. After a week of daily plastic feedings, his team saw gut tissue damage — but only in the low-fiber group. Experiments in test tubes suggest that fiber physically wraps around and sticks to plastic particles.

It’s too soon to say if dietary fiber does the same in humans. Zeng’s study was performed in mice and not tethered to realistic fiber numbers. Though mice in the high-fiber group ate far more fiber than what what’s recommended for people, he thinks the findings are worth pursuing in follow-up studies.

And even if fiber doesn’t end up purging plastic from people’s guts, Zeng says, it probably wouldn’t hurt for us to add a little more to our diets.

#6371. The 7 Best Car Battery Chargers for Roadside Emergencies

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Maintain your car battery—or bring a dead one back to life.

The 12-volt battery is one of the least complex components in modern vehicles but one of the most crucial. If it’s not in good condition, the engine won’t start, and none of the vehicle’s fancy systems will work. Car batteries have a limited lifecycle and deteriorate with time. This can happen for many reasons, including extended inactivity, extreme temperatures, or even something as simple as accidentally leaving the lights on after you turn off the engine.

That’s why it’s handy to have an external car battery charger so your engine is ready to go when you need it. A charger can also help extend your battery's life, for instance, in a vehicle you don't drive often—a weekend getaway camper or an old classic cruiser. Some chargers also have a jumpstart feature, eliminating the need for jumper cables (and the inconvenience of a required second vehicle).

You might be surprised to hear that electric vehicles use the same 12-volt car batteries as their internal combustion counterparts. Regardless, modern vehicles rely on this ancillary battery to power lights and onboard electronics when the ignition is off. Here, we’ve compiled the best chargers for cars and motorcycles, including everything from a solar-powered charger to a model that can revive several vehicles at once.

Noco’s Genius 10, the brand’s flagship single-vehicle charger, offers many cool features, including the ability to “force charge” a battery so dead it won't generate any voltage when you hook it up. (Most modern chargers won’t do this.) Maintenance and “desulfation” modes extend your battery's useful life while keeping it ready to go.

Unlike smaller, less ambitious chargers, the Genius 10 charges a vehicle battery to full power in the shortest safe time. It can even charge the new generation of lithium-ion car batteries, like the complex, expensive units fitted to many newer BMWs.

All the basic features are here at a very low price, including protection from reverse clamping and a “float mode” for fully charged batteries.

The included set of bolt-on leads lets you quickly connect and disconnect the charger. Operation couldn’t be simpler: a green light shows the Motopower is on, and a red light indicates charging status. With 1.5 amps of power, it charges slightly faster than most competitors in the low-price bracket.

Think of this 15-amp charger as a miniature version of the shop-grade Schumacher. It’s also the form and function that will be most familiar to older or experienced users. The included clamps are high-quality and should fit most cars. Just clamp on, plug in, and select one of three modes.

The 15-amp rapid charge is slightly more than the competition can manage, and a carrying handle makes it easy to place where you want it.

This charger is compact, light, easy to operate, and almost bombproof. It delivers a 3-amp charge, then automatically switches to float mode to maintain proper voltage and prevent overcharging.

A two-color LED indicates charging status, and if the battery voltage drops below a certain level, it resumes full charging output in adaptive mode. It’s compatible with most automotive batteries and can switch between 6- and 12-volt batteries with the push of a button. Its battery clamps are spark-proof, and the Battery Tender 3-Amp will automatically detect reverse polarity. It comes with a 5-year warranty and lifetime customer service.

Dealerships and race shops that used to scatter CTEK individual chargers throughout the building are now switching to the multi-vehicle Noco 2x4 model. It weighs just under 8 pounds, mounts to a wall, and can handle four vehicles at the same time, each in a different mode.

Want to float charge one car, recondition another, and bring two other dead batteries back to life in force-charge mode? Not a problem.

If you own a vehicle you only drive occasionally, an under-the-hood charger saves the hassle of disconnecting it from the battery and storing it each time you want to go for a cruise.

The compact Schumacher SC1300 mounts under the hood to supply up to 1.5 amps, while a built-in microprocessor automatically adjusts the charging rate to maintain an ideal charge state. Float mode delivers a small current when needed.

Reverse hook-up protection prevents the charger from working if the battery clamps are installed in reverse polarity, and the Schumacher automatically detects 6-volt or 12-volt batteries.

If an electrical outlet isn’t available or if you just want to use the sun to keep your battery topped off, the Sun Energize solar-powered charger is a reliable option. It trickle-charges a variety of automotive batteries, as well as some lithium batteries.

A built-in charge controller prevents overcharging; charging stops when a battery is topped off and automatically resumes when it drains.

An LED indicator shows charge and battery conditions. The 20.1 x 13.8 x 0.7-inch solar panel is larger than the other chargers here, but it’s built to handle high winds and heavy loads and is IP65 waterproof.

We tested some external battery chargers under varying weather conditions, while others were chosen based on feedback from car enthusiast friends. The selections represent a wide variety of chargers with different capabilities to match a broad range of use cases. We have years of experience traveling the country with these chargers and know their performance very well.

If you store a vehicle for long periods, you’ll want a charger to keep the battery from fully dying and turning into a paperweight. (It’s also nice to know it will start without jumper cables.) But a battery charger can make a difference in plenty of other situations.

If you regularly experience below-freezing temperatures at night, a charger with a maintenance function can significantly extend your battery's life. If you rarely drive more than a few miles at a time, a charger can prevent your battery from discharging too far—leaving you with a no-start condition. Last but not least, older vehicles often struggle to recharge slightly depleted batteries on the move, so starting the day with a fully charged battery can also extend the life of your alternator and charging system.

Charging power is traditionally measured in amps. Think of amps as the amount of juice that can be put back into the battery at any given time; for example, a 10-amp charger puts twice as much charge into the battery as a 5-amp one. A quick stroll through a listing of battery chargers can be confounding, though. Some have 40 amps, and some have 0.75 amps, and yet they do the same thing. In reality, the difference is easy to understand. The more power a charger has, the more quickly it can bring a dead battery back to life. The tradeoff is cost, size, and weight.

If you’re charging a small motorcycle battery or maintaining a good-condition battery in a cherished collector car, then a 0.75-amp charger will do just fine. If you’re worried that your pickup won’t start in the winter, 2 to 10 amps is a better bet. Any capability above that is mostly for mechanics who need to quickly charge or recondition batteries in the shop.

Every charger here can “maintain” a charged battery, keeping it from slowly discharging between uses. Most chargers can also bring a depleted battery back up to full power. A few chargers offer specialized modes like “desulfation,” which helps a battery regain its chemical balance through carefully timed charge-and-discharge cycles. A “quick charge” can very rapidly (but safely) prepare a battery for use. A few battery chargers also offer a “jump start mode” that can start a car or motorcycle with a dead battery, but this is rare, and most of the time you’ll need a separate jump starter for that task.

Most chargers in this roundup are designed for conventional lead-acid (flooded cell) or Absorbent Glass Mat (AGM) batteries, which you’ll find in newer vehicles. If you have a vehicle with a lithium-ion battery, like some new BMWs, or a customized car with ultra-compact batteries from manufacturers like Braille, you’ll need a charger with that capability—different battery chemistries require specific charging protocols.

If you are dealing with a cramped garage, or travel between storage spaces throughout the seasons, consider a “wall wart” or direct-mount charger. The former keeps all the charging mechanisms in a large plug that some people might compare to model-train transformer plugs. The latter bolts into your car and plugs directly into the wall.

Not anymore. Today's smart chargers, like the ones in our article, won't overcharge a battery or give it more than it can handle. And choosing a more powerful charger won't shorten your battery's lifespan; quite the opposite, in fact!

It's usually as simple as removing the bolt from both battery clamps, slipping the thin copper loops between the bolt and washer, and reinstalling. Then you can coil the quick-disconnect cord in a convenient place, like inside a motorcycle fairing or under a car hood. The cables can melt when exposed to serious heat, so don't let them touch an exhaust pipe.

Yes, if the batteries are in reasonably decent condition. Any charger rated at 2 Amps or more should be able to rotate between multiple vehicles. If you have more than three or four, consider buying multiple chargers.

#6370. A Simple Pill Could Cure a Common Cause of High Blood Pressure

Blood pressure stayed lower for up to two years after treatment ended in a small follow-up study, suggesting some people with hormone-driven hypertension could avoid lifelong medication.

For people with a common hormonal cause of high blood pressure, a cure has required surgery to remove an entire adrenal gland. Medication can keep their blood pressure under control, often with the prospect of taking it for life.

The condition, called primary aldosteronism, accounts for an estimated 5% to 10% of cases of high blood pressure, or hypertension, which affects millions of people worldwide. Benign nodules in the adrenal glands produce too much of the hormone aldosterone, causing the kidneys to retain excess salt and driving blood pressure up.

A study led by Queen Mary University of London now suggests that a limited course of medication could offer a lasting cure for some people with this condition. The approach, called extended aldosterone synthase inhibition (EASI), involves taking a new class of drugs for 6 to 12 months. These drugs block aldosterone synthase, an enzyme needed to make the hormone, targeting the excess production responsible for the hypertension.

The findings, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, came from follow-up measurements in 14 people treated at eight centers across the United States. They had participated in the first study of this drug class in people with primary aldosteronism, also led by Queen Mary and reported last year in the same journal. Researchers subsequently examined routine measurements of their blood pressure and hormone levels to see how they compared with values recorded before treatment.

For up to two years after treatment ended, hormone levels and blood pressure remained similar to, or lower than, those measured while participants were taking the drugs. The main marker of excess aldosterone production remained 99% below its pretreatment level, and blood pressure was, on average, 25 points lower. Researchers reported partial or complete resolution of hypertension, with almost a quarter of participants having normal blood pressure without taking any other medication.

Mason Freeman, Professor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School, initiated the original study while medical director at Cincor. He said, “This follow-up study led by Dr. Brown has generated some extraordinary and unexpected findings. The sustained remission in the biochemical markers of the hyperaldosterone state, combined with much improved blood pressure levels, offers the very exciting possibility that many patients with primary aldosteronism may be able to be treated with a once-a-day pill, perhaps for a limited period of time, and obtain similar benefits to what we now achieve only after invasive diagnostic testing and major adrenal surgery.”

Aldosterone synthase inhibitors had previously been tested in larger studies of people with hypertension. Those studies generally involved shorter treatment periods of 6 to 12 weeks, with outcomes measured while people were still taking the medication. Following patients after a 6- to 12-month course revealed the possibility that the treatment’s effects could outlast the medication itself.

One possible explanation dates to a 2005 experiment in mice. When scientists deleted the gene responsible for producing aldosterone synthase, the cells that make aldosterone disappeared. Researchers at Queen Mary predicted that blocking the enzyme for a prolonged period might have a similar effect in humans, potentially removing the source of excess hormone production.

Morris Brown, the study’s lead author and Professor of Endocrine Hypertension at Queen Mary, said, “While duly cautious about our findings because of the pragmatic nature of the study, they were predicted by previous experiments, and longer follow-up may justify a claim that a finite course of medication leads to infinite cure.

“EASI-treatment is unlikely to be the elixir for most patients with hypertension. But the possibility of tablets achieving a surgical cure has long been a holy grail for this common type of hypertension.”

The researchers are now leading a larger prospective clinical trial called ELIXIR to investigate whether EASI treatment can provide a lasting cure for people with primary aldosteronism. The trial will also use molecular imaging of the adrenal glands to examine whether prolonged treatment causes aldosterone-producing cells to disappear in humans.

Reference: “Hyperaldosteronism Remission after Extended Aldosterone Synthase Inhibition” by Morris J. Brown, Adina F. Turcu, Ramin Sam, Lawrence S. NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope could capture images 30% sharper than — and remain operational for twice as long as — initially expected. Researchers say these "remarkable" developments could greatly enhance the volume and quality of the data they will analyze.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is nearing its final destination more than 1 million miles (1.6 million kilometers) from Earth, where it will soon scour the universe for a host of cosmological treasures, including an estimated 100,000 new alien worlds.

But even before its mission truly begins, recent developments suggest the state-of-the-art spacecraft could take better images than — and remain operational for more than twice as long as — initially expected, further delighting already-excited astronomers.

"It is fantastic to learn that Roman is not just reaching its design goals but exceeding them," Eamonn Kerins, an astronomer at the University of Manchester in the U.K. who will help lead one of Roman's major surveys, told Live Science.

Roman is NASA's latest flagship space telescope, following in the footsteps of iconic observatories like the Hubble Space Telescope and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The $4 billion machine ‪—‬ which is over 42 feet (12.7 meters) long and weighs around the same as a fully grown Tyrannosaurus rex ‪—‬ successfully launched into space on Aug. 30, more than a decade after scientists started building it.

The telescope is now en route to Lagrange point 2 (L2), a fixed point relative to our planet where Earth's gravity and the sun's gravity cancel each other out. There, Roman will join several other important spacecraft, including JWST and the European Space Agency's Euclid telescope.

Roman was launched into space on board one of SpaceX's Falcon heavy rockets. It lifted off Aug. 30 from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

During Roman's journey to L2, which is currently around 85% complete, mission scientists have remotely switched on the telescope's various instruments to test whether they function as expected. So far, this "commissioning process" has gone off without a hitch, and by the time Roman arrives in less than two weeks, it should be ready to snap its first in-depth images of the cosmos.

Researchers were already pumped to see what Roman will be able to do once it is in place and fully switched on. However, that excitement has further intensified in recent weeks, thanks to two postlaunch developments.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

First, a series of near-perfect rocket burns, executed during and shortly after launch, saved more than a decade's worth of fuel that can now be used to extend Roman's mission. Second, after remotely adjusting the telescope's mirror, researchers discovered it should be capable of snapping images with around 30% greater detail than engineers predicted.

The team that designed, launched and remotely commissioned the orbital observatory has "done an amazing job" and "their work has ensured that Roman is more than up to the task," Kerins said.

Shortly after Roman arrived in space on board a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket that lifted off from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, mission scientists conducted two major burns, or engine firings, which gave the spacecraft enough momentum to escape Earth's orbit and make the journey to L2.

Roman is around the same size as a small truck and was packed into the nose cone of the Falcon Heavy rocket prior to launch.

Thanks to a combination of "exquisite planning by our orbital dynamics team" and "brilliant execution by the operations team," these burns were so precise that each one saved up to four years' worth of fuel, Jamie Dunn, director of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, said in a Sept. 14 statement.

On top of this, Roman ended up being much lighter than initially planned, which allowed engineers to pack another four years' worth of fuel into the spacecraft before launch. "Since Roman's [weight] was lower than we budgeted for, we were able to fill the propellant tanks to their capacity rather than only filling them as much as we needed," Alison Rao, the Roman propulsion lead at NASA Goddard, said in the statement.

In total, these savings could give Roman an additional 12 years of fuel, which could more than double the mission's planned 10-year lifespan. That means Roman could still be capturing images of the cosmos in 2048.

Given that Roman can collect data up to 1,000 times faster than Hubble, this extended lifespan will greatly enhance the amount of data the new space telescope will be able to capture. "With a 20-year Roman lifetime, we could, in theory, do over 20,000 years of Hubble survey work," Kerins said. "That's a lot of science!"

Roman is now on its way to L2, where the gravity of Earth and the sun cancel out, allowing it to remain in one place without expending much fuel.

This prolonged lifespan will let astronomers compare images of specific objects decades apart — such as expanding nebulas or colliding galaxies — allowing them to detect changes they otherwise might have missed.

It may also let them study objects or phenomena that we haven't even discovered yet, which is particularly exciting, Kerins noted. "The real show-stopper results will be new things we just aren't even thinking about right now," he said. "The possibilities are truly breathtaking."

There is also the chance that Roman's mission could be extended even further, because engineers often find clever ways of making active spacecraft last longer. For example, Hubble is more than two decades past its initial mission parameters, and the recently deceased Swift Observatory lasted 10 times longer than initially predicted before falling back to Earth last week.

Roman's secret weapon is arguably its Wide Field Instrument (WFI), made up of a 288-megapixel camera attached to a 7.9-foot (2.4 m) mirror, which will capture ultra-detailed images with a field of view roughly 100 times larger than Hubble's.

Roman's WFI consists of a 288-megapixel camera attached to a 7.9-foot (2.4 m) mirror. It will be capable of capturing images with a field of view 100 times greater than Hubble.

We have already seen the first WFI images — a series of blurry, green dots captured during a test of the instrument's 18 different light detectors ( see below). However, those photos were nothing like what WFI will capture in the future; those images will be so detailed that you would need dozens of high-definition TVs to properly display a single snap in full resolution, Kerins said.

After Roman completes the initial WFI commissioning phase, those images will be around 30% sharper than designers predicted. "All of the images from Roman's cosmic surveys will be even sharper than we expected," Alden Jurling, a senior optical engineer who works on Roman at NASA Goddard, said in an Oct. 14 statement. "It's a great outcome."

The improvements were first noticed after the WFI's car-sized mirror was realigned by just one-sixteenth the diameter of a human hair, demonstrating just how intricate the commissioning process has been. "Calibrating an instrument is like tuning a piano or guitar before a concert," Maxime Rizzo, a WFI systems engineer at NASA Goddard, said in the statement. "You adjust everything until it's just how you want it and then leave the settings alone so it performs consistently while you use it."

NASA released Roman's first photos on Sept. 15. Each small square represents one of the telescope's light detectors, and each blurry green spot is a distant star. (This is just a test image and does not represent how the telescope's proper photos will look.)

The improved image quality could really come to the fore during Roman's hunt for potentially habitable exoplanets, which is what Live Science's readers are most excited about for this mission.

Kerins, who is leading the Exoplanet Demographics Working Group for the Transits in the Roman Exoplanets Survey, is particularly excited about this development, but he said it does not necessarily guarantee that Roman will find more exoplanets than initially predicted.

The rest of Roman's commissioning phase is also proceeding as planned.

Roman's coronagraph instrument, which will block out the light from distant stars to allow WFI to spot alien worlds, has passed its main commissioning phase and is working as intended, according to a NASA blog post.

Roman has completed around 85% of its journey to L2 and should arrive at its final destination in the next few weeks. (The timeline in this image is a screenshot from Roman's commissioning process website, captured on Nov. 11.)

Meanwhile, a global network of ground stations, which will receive up to 1.4 terabytes of data from Roman every day, has established contact with the spacecraft and is receiving signals as expected, another blog post revealed.

All of these early wins raise hopes that Roman can have a long and successful career, and are a testament to the years of work that went into designing the spacecraft and planning the mission.

"What we're seeing now with the actual optical performance and estimated lifetime of Roman is just how good that design process has been," Kerins said. "It's a remarkable achievement. I can't wait to see what Roman is going to give us."

Harry is a U.K.-based senior staff writer at Live Science. He studied marine biology at the University of Exeter before training to become a journalist. He covers a wide range of topics including space exploration, planetary science, space weather, climate change, animal behavior and paleontology. His recent work on the solar maximum won "best space submission" at the 2024 Aerospace Media Awards and was shortlisted in the "top scoop" category at the NCTJ Awards for Excellence in 2023. He also writes Live Science's weekly Earth from space series.

#6368. Scientists Develop Injectable Glucose Sensor That Could Change Diabetes Care

An experimental injectable sensor could give people with diabetes a more affordable way to track blood sugar, with early tests showing that a cheaper sensing ingredient performed similarly to its costlier alternative.

For millions of people with diabetes, knowing how glucose levels are changing helps guide decisions about medication, meals, and daily activities. Continuous glucose monitors provide that information in real time, but their cost keeps the devices out of reach for some patients. Making monitoring more affordable requires attention to the materials inside a sensor, as well as how reliably they work.

Researchers at Texas A&M University have identified a less expensive ingredient for an experimental injectable glucose sensor. Their study, published in ACS Measurement Science AU, found that a sensing material costing roughly one-tenth as much as an alternative used in earlier versions delivered comparable performance.

The proposed sensor houses its sensing chemistry in a small hydrogel, a water-rich material that can be injected into tissue and sit beneath the skin. The gel provides a stable home for the sensing materials while allowing glucose to pass through. In testing, it retained more than 94% of the sensing mixture over seven days, demonstrating that the chemistry could function within an injectable platform.

“Our long-term goal is to develop a reliable, affordable injectable glucose sensor that can expand access to continuous glucose monitoring, particularly for people in under-resourced communities and those without adequate insurance coverage,” said Dr. Gérard L. Coté, the study’s principal investigator and a professor of biomedical engineering in Texas A&M’s College of Engineering. “Reducing the cost of the sensing materials is one step toward making these technologies accessible to more people who need them.”

To measure glucose, the platform uses changes in near-infrared fluorescence, a light signal beyond the visible range. Many glucose-monitoring systems rely on enzymes, which help chemical reactions occur. This approach instead detects glucose through a competition between molecules.

Glucose and a fluorescent sugar compound compete for available binding sites on a protein called concanavalin A, or ConA. As glucose concentrations rise, more glucose molecules enter that competition, changing the fluorescent signal. This process, known as competitive binding, allows the researchers to track glucose concentrations without enzymes.

The team compared several glucose-binding compounds, including two forms of a sugar called mannopentaose. Earlier versions of the technology used α-mannopentaose. The much less expensive β-mannopentaose provided comparable sensing performance and also performed well in artificial interstitial fluid, a solution designed to mimic the environment beneath the skin.

“The surprising part was how closely the lower-cost material matched the performance of the more expensive alternative,” said Dr. Sayantan Tripathy, an assistant research scientist in Texas A&M’s Optical and Bio-Sensing Laboratory and the study’s lead author. “In this case, the cheaper option wasn’t really a compromise, and that’s an important finding when you’re thinking about future glucose-monitoring technologies.”

The cost comparison concerns one sensing component. The technology remains at the proof-of-concept stage and needs additional development and testing before it could be considered for clinical use.

“Developing an affordable glucose sensor means considering the cost of the individual materials as well as how well they work together,” Coté said. “This study shows that we can substantially reduce the cost of one sensing component while maintaining comparable performance, giving us a promising foundation for further development.”

Reducing manufacturing costs could eventually help expand access to future diabetes-monitoring technologies. That possibility makes affordability a consideration throughout development, alongside technical performance.

“When new medical technologies are expensive, access can be limited,” said Dr. Melissa Grunlan, a study co-author, professor of biomedical engineering in the College of Engineering, and professor of chemistry in the College of Arts and Sciences. “Our goal is to develop sensors that are not only effective but affordable for the people who rely on them.”

The team plans to refine the platform and evaluate additional components that may improve its performance, longevity, and practicality.

“While the work remains in the research stage, the findings suggest that future glucose-monitoring technologies may not have to rely on expensive materials to deliver effective results,” Tripathy said.

Reference: “β-Anomeric Mannopentaose-Based Nonenzymatic NIR Glucose Sensor Enabling Cost-Effective Continuous Monitoring” by Sayantan Tripathy, Diana Al Husseini, Carolina I. Martinez, Anthony Dongchau, Samyucktha Ganesapandian, Melissa A Grunlan and Gerard L Cote, 19 August 2026, ACS Measurement Science Au. DOI: 10.1021/acsmeasuresciau.6c00076

This research was funded by the National Science Foundation (NSF) Engineering Research Center for Precise Advanced Technologies and Health Systems for Under-resourced Populations.

#6367. The 5 Best Gas Snowblowers Can Move Mountains (of Snow)

Too much snow to shovel? A snowblower offers the most power and the longest runtime.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Winter will be here before you know it, which means the best time to prepare for cold weather and potential snowstorms is now. While snowfall isn't as regular in many parts of the country as it used to be, storm systems can still dump big piles of snow at once. When it comes time to dig out, there are few tools as effective as a gas-powered snowblower.

Although electric snowblowers are certainly attractive—they are relatively lightweight, easy to use, and require little maintenance—they lack the raw power and long runtime you’ll need if a storm drops 18 inches of snow or more on your home, especially if you have a large driveway.

The best gas snowblowers can carve a path as wide as two feet—giving you plenty of room to walk through as much as 21 inches of snow on a single pass. And if you keep a spare tank handy, you should have more than enough runtime to clear your walks and driveway multiple times. If you’re in the market for a heavy-duty snow removal machine, we’ve researched and tested plenty. These are our top picks, plus a breakdown of everything you need to know to pick out the best gas snowblower for your home.

If you have a large driveway and get a lot of snow, this is the machine you want. This big Ariens has a 30-inch-wide clearing path and an ideal clearing depth of 18 inches. Its four-stroke gas engine means no fussing with mixed fuel, and the push-button electric start means you don't have to exhaust yourself with a recoil starter.

This is a stout machine that is made for working. Test Editor Brad Ford runs a similar machine on his property, which is extra demanding because he has a gravel driveway. Thankfully, this machine can handle gravel surfaces thanks to its adjustable skid shoes, which allow extra clearance between the base of the auger and the driveway.

This machine is not for everybody; smaller properties will be well-served by the smaller picks below. But for those with the capacity for this kind of snowblower, this Ariens is a solid choice.

This model from Champion Power Equipment lists at $899, which is a good price point considering many two-stage snowblowers are more than $1,000. But it’s not short on features. This model gives you push-button electric start, a self-propelled drive system, remote chute control, and an LED headlight for clearing snow at night. After all, the snow doesn’t always stop falling during work hours.

It also handles fairly deep snowfall with a 24-inch width and a 20.5-inch height. To help keep the blades safe on uneven terrain, you can adjust the height to handle that, or clear areas like gravel paths. Another feature we really like is the ability to turn the wheels 180 degrees to help make tighter turns. Features like that can’t always be found at this price point, which is why it’s our pick for a snowblower that packs a lot of value.

A medium-sized property that only gets a moderate amount of guaranteed snowfall each year doesn’t need a two-stage snowblower. A single-stage model is fully capable of clearing your driveway and sidewalks. This model from Toro has plenty of power to get that job done, with a 212-cc engine that should cut through even wet snow and throw it up to 35 feet away. This model is also self-propelled to help you do the pushing.

Some of the features we like on it are a trigger and slide that can change the direction of the discharge chute from the handle and a push-button electric start—both make operating it a little bit easier.

Like most single-stage snowblowers, its intake is lower than a two-stage, so you can only expect to clear snowfall up to 10 inches. If you commonly get much higher than that, you’ll want a more robust snowblower, but if you only have a few moderate snow events each winter, this Toro will get the job done.

The Toro SnowMaster 824 QXE stands apart from other single-stage gas snowblowers because of its intuitive controls and powerful engine. With a 252-cc engine, it chews rapidly through snow, carving a 24-inch path through banks up to 18 inches high.

With a lighter, more compact frame and automatic steering, the 824 QXE is easier to maneuver than its dual-stage counterparts. And, unlike most single-stage snowblowers, the auger is slightly elevated, so you can use it on gravel surfaces without having to worry about sucking rocks into it.

This machine also brings lots of special features to make the clearing process easier. Not only is it self-propelled, but it features a “personal pace system” that automatically adjusts the snowblower’s speed to match your walking pace, so you don’t have to fumble with speed controls. If you're familiar with Toro's self-propelled lawn mowers, this system should be familiar.

The snowblower also has a push-button starter and joystick-operated chute control, which makes it easy to adjust your snow output on the fly. If you’re looking for a snowblower to clear up to 18 inches of snow from a small to medium-sized driveway, the SnowMaster 824 QXE is a worthy choice.

This snowblower from Murray is another great example of a two-stage snowblower from a respected company that doesn’t cost more than $1,000. It doesn’t have some of the extra features like our best value pick—namely, a headlight and a 180-degree wheel rotation—but it otherwise matches it in size and power.

It also has all the primary features you would want, including an adjustable chute that lets you aim the snow where you want, push-button electric start, an auger that can propel snow up to 40 feet away, and a self-propel drive with six forward speeds and two reverse speeds.

Something unique to the model, however, is a set of 15-inch snow-terrain tires that handle icy and rocky conditions better than others. Wheels are something other brands can skimp on, but Murray hasn’t done that here. If you have gravel paths or older sidewalks that present a challenge, this model is likely up to the task.

Gas snowblowers are the best tools for heavy-duty snow removal jobs at home. They’re effective against snowbanks piled up to two feet high, and can clear out larger areas, including wide driveways and walking paths. If you live somewhere that gets hit by many large snowstorms each season, and you’ve got a considerable-sized area to clear, then this is what you need.

Not everyone needs a gas snowblower, though. For homes with smaller needs, they may feel like more trouble than they’re worth. Gas-powered machines require more maintenance. Plus, they’re usually quite heavy, which makes them hard to use on tiered walkways with steps. If heavy snow is a rare occurrence, we’d recommend going with an electric snowblower instead, which will be more nimble and won’t produce any fumes.

Most gas snowblowers feature either a single-stage or two-stage mechanism, depending on how the snowblower collects, processes, and expels snow.

Also known as “snow throwers,” they use an auger to pull in snow, break it up, and throw the snow out through the chute in a single action.

These also use an auger to pull in snow, but then mash it up with a spinning impeller before spitting it out through the chute. Separating the snow-pulling and snow-crushing/throwing mechanisms allows the two-stage snowblowers to move snow more quickly and throw it a longer distance, which can be helpful when clearing larger driveways. These robust machines also work better on gravel, since their augers are slightly elevated and won’t draw rocks into the tines.

With an extra component that requires a more powerful engine to operate properly, two-stage snowblowers are generally larger, making them more difficult to maneuver around tight spaces. If you have a small walkway or gardens with uneven ground to avoid, operating one may feel unwieldy. As you might expect, they also cost more than their single-stage counterparts.

As with deciding between electric and gas snowblowers, consider the size of the area you normally clear before picking a single- or two-stage model. Single-stage snowblowers work well for clearing walking paths and the average-sized two- to four-car paved driveway. Dual-stage models are ideal for clearing deep snow from long paved or gravel driveways.

A snowblower’s clearing width and intake height determine how much snow it can move with each pass. The larger the snowblower’s intake, the more quickly you can get the job done.

Most single-stage gas-powered snowblowers have intakes that range from 22 to 24 inches wide, while two-stage snowblowers can have intakes that are up to 32 inches wide. The height of the snowblower’s intake, which is sometimes referred to as “clearing depth,” indicates the maximum snow depth it can handle. The intake height for a gas snowblower ranges from 18 to 21 inches.

Purchasing the snowblower with the widest, tallest intake may seem like a no-brainer, but keep in mind that there’s a correlation between intake dimensions and the overall size of the snowblower. The largest gas snowblowers will have a harder time maneuvering through tight turns. Ultimately, you should choose the smallest option that can effectively clear the paths you need and the amount of snow you expect to see.

A snowblower's job is to take snow in front of you and move it somewhere out of the way. With a more powerful snowblower, you can send the snow farther away. That’s crucial when you’re clearing out a large space, and you need to pile it up dozens of feet from you. Single-stage gas snowblowers can launch snow up to 40 feet, while two-stage snowblowers have a snow-throwing range of 50 feet or more.

Some gas snowblowers come equipped with a throttle on the dashboard that allows you to adjust the throwing distance by changing the speed of the impeller, allowing you to target a specific snow-piling plot.

Beyond the basics, many gas snowblowers have additional features that make them easier to use. Since they weigh hundreds of pounds, many are self-propelled, so you don’t have to push them forward. Most also have electric starters that eliminate the need to pull a starter cord. Some even have built-in power steering that automatically slows one wheel for easy turning.

Other quality-of-life features abound: You may find dashboard controls that allow you to change the chute direction and snowblower speed with one hand, LED headlights for late-night (or early morning) jobs, and handlebars that heat up to keep your hands nice and toasty as you work.

We selected the best gas snowblowers based on recommendations from the Popular Mechanics test team, as well as research and personal testing experience. Some of our picks were recommended by Popular Mechanics test editor Brad Ford, who has logged hours and hours testing snowblowers over the years. The final lineup includes a mix of single-stage gas-powered models for small to moderate driveways that can house four to six cars, and larger two-stage models that can clear snow from the longer and larger driveways you usually find on rural properties.

There are a few things you need to do to make sure your gas snowblower runs smoothly through the season:

First, check the oil level between each use and top off as needed. You should change the oil once a year, even if you didn’t use your snowblower all winter.

Change the spark plug at the beginning of each season to ensure it starts smoothly. A dirty spark plug can make it difficult to get your snowblower going, especially in extreme cold.

Lastly, small gas engines require plenty of airflow to run smoothly, so check the air filter once a season and replace it if it's dirty.

Snowblowers use unleaded gasoline—the same thing you put in your car—which begins to degrade after about 60 days. Running a snowblower with old fuel can clog the carburetor and make the engine hard to start, so you should never store your snowblower with fuel left in the tank.

Before putting your snowblower to bed for the season, either run the fuel tank dry or add fuel stabilizer, which keeps gasoline fresh for up to 24 months, to the tank. If you use fuel stabilizer, run the snowblower for a minute or two after adding it to the tank to circulate it through the engine.

A snowblower should be able to handle the lion’s share of your snow removal duties, but you should definitely keep a snow shovel around to clean up whatever the snowblower leaves behind. You may also want to save the gas and dig out with a shovel after a light, soft snowfall.

#6366. Drugs like Ozempic may help reverse chronic kidney disease

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Semaglutide helped repair blood vessels and reduce inflammation in the kidneys, a study finds

A patient undergoes hemodialysis, a process that filters waste from blood when the kidneys can’t. A new study shows how the popular weight loss drug semaglutide can help repair damaged kidneys.

Maria Symchych-Navrotska/iStock/Getty Images Plus

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ozempic’s key ingredient fixes faulty filters in the kidney.

The well-known weight loss drug repairs and restores blood vessels that power people’s waste disposal systems, researchers report October 1 in Nature Medicine. Those actions mean the ingredient, called semaglutide, can add another notch to its list of health benefits: treating chronic kidney disease.

In patients with the condition, semaglutide also increased blood flow and tamped down inflammation, the team found. The study reinforces the GLP-1 drug’s known anti-inflammatory effects, while also suggesting that it may play a direct role in protecting the kidney’s blood vessels, says Susan Quaggin, a nephrologist at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago who was not involved in the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Chronic kidney disease affects an estimated 674 million people worldwide, with some of the most common causes being diabetes and high blood pressure. As the disease progresses, the kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter out waste from blood and excrete it as urine. This causes other health complications, as well as a sharply increased risk of dying from a heart attack or stroke.

Patients with diabetic chronic kidney disease who took semaglutide were less likely to wind up in kidney failure, or die from a heart attack or stroke, than those taking a placebo, researchers reported in 2024 in the New England Journal of Medicine. That trial was stopped early, as the drug was so effective at preventing death that doctors no longer considered it ethical to keep giving participants the placebo.

For the new study, some of those same researchers then looked at a subset of 106 participants to find out how the drug worked. The team collected kidney tissue samples before and after the participants took semaglutide, and compared them with samples from participants given the placebo. Semaglutide use led to striking visible changes in the tissues, including increased blood flow, reduced scarring and reduced blood vessel stiffness, a measure of vessel health.

Increased blood flow is important because it increases filtration, which is the kidneys’ main job, says Peter Nguyen, a nephrologist at Houston Methodist Hospital who was not involved in the study.

Researchers also looked at levels of a protein, called albumin, in patients’ urine. High levels can be an early sign that the kidneys’ filters aren’t working well. While those levels didn’t change much in those on the placebo, they dropped in patients taking semaglutide ― a sign the filters weren’t quite as leaky any more.

The team then looked under the hood for genetic clues to how semaglutide appeared to heal the kidneys. Within the glomerulus, the tiny blood vessels responsible for the kidney’s filtering action, genes relating to metabolic stress were turned off, Katherine Tuttle, a nephrologist at the University of Washington’s Providence Medical Research Center in Spokane, and colleagues found. Within these same cells, inflammatory genes were also turned off, while repair genes were switched on.

The researchers also looked at a subset of genes responsible for cells “talking” to each other within the glomerulus. Before semaglutide, the blood vessels and immune cells were “chattering” with each other, sending lots of inflammatory signals, Tuttle says. After semaglutide, the immune cells went quiet, silencing the messages that ramp up harmful inflammation. These changes in gene activity point to a healthier kidney that’s less stressed and inflamed, and that has had repair processes flipped on.

With semaglutide treatment, Tuttle says, patients’ damaged kidneys showed clear signs of repair.

A new study supports a more nuanced approach to obesity diagnosis. Here's what to know.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Obesity is linked to a range of health problems ‪—‬ including heart disease, diabetes and early death ‪—‬ but it can be hard to know who is most at risk for these outcomes. Doctors and researchers often use body mass index (BMI) as a convenient tool to assess patients, but this metric does not account for individual differences in body composition, scientists have long argued.

"BMI misses a lot of information," Dr. Francesco Rubino, a professor of bariatric and metabolic surgery at King's College London, told Live Science.

Rubino recently chaired a team of 56 experts that was assembled to better define obesity and develop new diagnostic criteria for the condition. First proposed in January 2025, their new framework includes more body measurements beyond BMI and distinguishes between "preclinical" and "clinical" obesity.

Now, a new study published Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Nature confirms that these new criteria could detect obesity with greater precision than BMI alone. In other words, with the new approach, more people would be accurately diagnosed with obesity and fewer people would be misdiagnosed than are with BMI alone.

Live Science spoke with Rubino and other experts to break down the new findings and learn what they mean for patients.

At the simplest level, obesity is excess body fat. There are special scans and exams that send weak electrical signals through the body to measure a person's body fat percentage directly, but criteria based on body measurements are more accessible across clinical settings.

BMI is the most common of these measurements, as it simply involves dividing a person's weight by their height squared. However, it does not account for individual differences in lean muscle mass or bone density.

BMI doesn't capture nuances and variation between patients, experts argue, and it limits what doctors can say about a given person's health risk.

Additionally, the different BMI categories — such as "overweight" and "obese" — don't carry the same risks for all patients. Certain racial and ethnic groups tend to experience health consequences, such as higher mortality rates, at different BMI levels than others do.

For a given patient being assessed for obesity, the proposed guidelines would suggest using at least one additional body measurement alongside BMI and having their doctor review their medical history for other signs of bodily or organ dysfunction.

The proposed body measurements are less influenced by a person's muscle mass or bone structure than BMI is. They include waist circumference, waist-to-hip ratio and waist-to-height ratio. Notably, because different ethnicities are associated with different fat distribution patterns in the body, the latest Nature study incorporated different waist circumference cutoffs based that varied by ethnicity.

In addition to these body measurements, the proposed criteria look at 18 conditions and signs of bodily or organ dysfunction that are related to obesity, such as cardiovascular diseases, joint pain and sleep apnea. (All 18 factors can be found detailed in this chart.)

Rubino and his colleagues — which together made up what's known as a Lancet Commission — defined "clinical obesity" as a disease state involving at least one of 18 forms of bodily dysfunction caused by excess fat tissue. Preclinical obesity, by contrast, is when a person is at risk of this disease state and may need interventions to avoid obesity-related dysfunction.

That means that two people with the same BMI, waist circumference and waist-to-height ratio may be classified differently, depending on whether they have other conditions. In the new study, between 77% and 91% of individuals with preclinical obesity did not progress to clinical obesity within 10 years, depending on the cohort analyzed.

This distinction can be complicated, though, as the diagnostic metrics for each form of dysfunction contain their own ambiguities.

"There needs to be more consensus on what's actually defining clinical obesity," said Dr. Aayush Visaria, an internal medicine instructor at Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School in New Jersey. Visaira was not involved in writing the new criteria but authored an analysis of the proposed measures.

The Lancet Commission argues that the categories of preclinical and clinical obesity could help doctors identify the people with the greatest need for treatment. The researchers tracked health outcomes using electronic health records from China, the United Kingdom, the United States and Spain, and they determined that their clinical obesity classification was better at flagging people's risk of death than BMI alone.

Changing the diagnostic criteria for obesity could, in turn, change who is recommended to receive weight-control medications.

They found no clear association between BMI and mortality risk, but clinical obesity was linked to a 69% greater risk of all-cause mortality, compared to no obesity.

The Lancet Commission's approach could drive a small net uptick in individuals diagnosed with obesity, according to the new study.

Under the current framework, "we are definitely missing some people who actually need obesity treatment but just did not meet the BMI criteria," said Dr. Jennifer Hwang, an instructor of medicine at the University of Chicago who has published her own analysis of the new criteria.

With the BMI-only approach, people with BMIs of 30 or higher are categorized as obese. With the new definition, some people with BMIs under 30 would be newly categorized as clinically obese, while a smaller group of people with high BMIs would suddenly not count as clinically obese, the Nature study predicted.

For instance, the former group might include people who have "overweight" BMIs but also have obesity-related dysfunction, while the latter group might include people with "obese" BMIs but without any dysfunction.

Overall, the new criteria would increase obesity prevalence by about 3.3% to 7.4%, the team predicted. The percentage varied depending on the group analyzed.

More research is needed to prove that the Lancet Commission's criteria would improve patient care and be practical to use in a clinical setting, Hwang said. She noted potential challenges in implementing both new aspects of the new framework. While the body measurements sound simple enough to use, clinicians would need training to perform them accurately.

Providers also may struggle with the new distinction between preclinical and clinical obesity. A 2025 analysis of the Lancet Commission framework noted that some patients who qualify for obesity medications under the Food and Drug Administration's guidelines may be recharacterized as having preclinical obesity and no longer receive a prescription.

Rubino and the rest of the Lancet Commission plan to continue validating their framework to see how it could best support personalized obesity treatment. For instance, they want to determine which forms of organ dysfunction are of greatest concern and develop a way of scoring each patient's level of risk.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Validation of clinical and preclinical obesity across global cohorts. Nature, 659. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11237-5
