#6352. Toxic secrets are hiding in Arctic ice

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A century-old pollution trail leads scientists back to Montana mining

At the turn of the twentieth century, the Anaconda Smelter in Montana spewed arsenic into the air — those heavy metal particles that are now trapped in Arctic ice cores.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ice cores record Earth’s secrets, even the dirty ones.

Some of the cylindrical sections of ice extracted from the Arctic contain elevated levels of arsenic, lead and other heavy metals that circulated in our planet’s atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Those pollutants, which have been tied to declines in IQ and higher rates of certain cancers, were probably emitted by a mining and smelting company in Montana whose grounds are now designated as multiple Superfund sites, the researchers report November 3 in Nature Sustainability.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The ice cores contain tiny particles that were once airborne — including pollutants, volcanic ash and salt from ocean spray — and fell to our planet’s surface within a few days or weeks. In polar regions, that fallout combines with snow and is preserved as ice.

Joseph McConnell, an environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, and his collaborators recently analyzed 10 ice cores collected across Canada, Greenland and Russia. The cores contained material that had fallen to Earth as early as 210 BCE, but the interval spanning the Industrial Revolution in the United States — from roughly 1870 to 1914 — was what caught the team’s collective eye.

In the ice layers from that period, arsenic concentrations in some of the ice cores were up to 15 times higher than pre-Industrial Revolution levels. Because the heavy metal exposure has been tied to upticks in the rates of certain cancers, McConnell and his team set out to determine the most likely source of all that pollution.

The largest increases in arsenic existed in the ice cores from Greenland. That finding was a big hint, McConnell says, because atmospheric circulation patterns tend to move material from west to east. “The only way you can explain that pattern of deposition is if the emissions are coming from North America,” McConnell says. “Had it been from Europe, we would have seen much larger increases in the Russian Arctic.”

The most likely source, the team concluded, was a massive copper mining and smelting operation in southwestern Montana operated by the Anaconda Copper Mining Company. It was one of the largest in North America during the Industrial Revolution and, unlike other copper mining operations in the area, it worked with copper ore that contained heavy metals like arsenic and lead. It was no secret that those toxic metals were entering the atmosphere, says Fred Quivik, a historian and the author of Smoke and Tailings, a book about the environmental history of copper smelting in Montana. “Ranchers and farmers started seeing their livestock die from arsenic poisoning.”

Based on the concentrations of arsenic in the ice cores and models of how material disperses in the atmosphere, McConnell and his colleagues estimated that the Anaconda Copper Mining Company was emitting roughly 30 tons of arsenic per day into the atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. By comparison, Chile, currently the world’s largest producer of copper and home to more than 20 mining operations, collectively emits roughly one quarter as much arsenic today.

Beginning in 1919, the Anaconda Copper Mining Company installed devices near its smokestacks and other facilities to capture arsenic and prevent its release into the atmosphere. Arsenic emissions dropped by about 60 percent as a result, the ice core data showed, but by then hundreds of thousands of nearby residents had already been exposed for decades. That exposure could have been lessened, McConnell says, if the Anaconda Copper Mining Company hadn’t waited so long to install the pollution-abatement technology. “They delayed installation for about a decade.”

These new findings should be combined with census records to trace the effects of this pollution on human health in the 19th and 20th centuries, McConnell and his team suggest. “We hope that epidemiologists will take this information and really investigate potential impacts on human populations.”

#6351. City squirrels seem to be thriving, but their genes tell a different story

Berlin’s red squirrels show subtle genetic differences across nearby green spaces, raising questions about how freely they move through the city.

Eurasian red squirrels are a familiar sight in the parks and gardens of Berlin, where they often appear to be perfectly at home.

Yet the roads and buildings lying between these green spaces may be making it harder for the animals to mix.

In a study of squirrels at three sites across the city, small genetic differences were found between groups living only a few miles apart. Survival, on the other hand, was much the same in all three places.

The findings reveal subtle genetic differences between groups, even though researchers detected no clear differences in survival.

The work was led by Sinah Drenske of the Leibniz Institute for Zoo and Wildlife Research (Leibniz-IZW), and wild squirrels were followed for close to four years.

“We do not see any highly isolated populations,” said Drenske. “But we are already detecting subtle genetic differences that suggest that squirrels cannot move completely freely through the city.”

All three sites have plenty of trees, but they differ in how built-up they are and how many people visit.

The quietest was a woodland area of about 94 acres (38 hectares) on the city’s outskirts, part of a much larger forest.

A cemetery of about 25 acres (10 hectares), surrounded by homes, parks and other cemeteries, fell in the middle.

At the other extreme was a city park of about 237 acres (96 hectares), crossed and bordered by major roads.

How crowded was each site? Walkers, dogs, bicycles and other activity along the paths were counted by observers in half-hour blocks. By this measure, the park was roughly 16 times as busy as the woodland.

Live traps baited with walnuts were set from autumn 2021 to spring 2025, over eight spring and autumn trapping periods of about six weeks each.

Each new squirrel was fitted with a small tag under the skin of its shoulder (so that it could be recognized later).

A tiny sample of ear tissue was also taken for DNA testing before the animal was let go.

Altogether, 141 squirrels were caught, one of them on 19 separate occasions.

The amount of variety in a population’s genes is known as its genetic diversity. It’s the raw material a population needs in order to adapt to change.

For 135 of the squirrels, genetic profiles were built from 16 stretches of DNA that commonly vary from one animal to the next.

Levels of diversity were broadly similar at all three sites. In fact, they were higher than the values reported for several squirrel populations in France, Great Britain and the island of Jersey.

There was, therefore, no sign that life in the city had sharply reduced the genetic variety of the squirrels (and inbreeding levels were low as well).

A closer look did turn up small differences, however. Individual squirrels in the busy park carried less genetic variety, on average, than those living in the woodland.

Such differences were read by the researchers as an early stage of genetic separation rather than a sign of serious isolation.

In the Japanese city of Obihiro, a 2024 study had found lower genetic diversity in city red squirrels than in rural ones. Compared with that result, the effects in Berlin were described by the authors as considerably weaker.

Three genetic groups had been expected, one for each site. Instead, only two were found by a computer analysis that sorts animals according to how genetically similar they are.

Most of the squirrels in the cemetery belonged to one of these groups, while most of those in the park belonged to the other. Yet the two sites are less than 2.5 miles (4 kilometers) apart.

In the woodland, about 12 miles (20 kilometers) from the cemetery, the squirrels carried a mix of both genetic backgrounds.

“If one considered only the geographical location, one would have expected the populations in the city park and the cemetery – which are just a few kilometers apart – to be genetically similar, whilst the forest population, which is significantly further away, would stand out more,” Drenske said.

Because close relatives can make a population look more divided than it really is, 35 closely related squirrels (21 of them from the park) were taken out of the data.

When the analysis was run again, two groups still appeared, although the split between them was weaker.

Earlier work on hedgehogs in Berlin had a different outcome, as an apparent genetic split vanished there once relatives had been taken into account.

Researchers believe squirrels from the woodland may have moved into the two city areas. Over time, limited movement between these places could have increased their genetic differences.

Berlin’s wide roads, railways, and waterways may make it harder for squirrels to travel between green spaces.

An earlier computer model suggested that the park could connect the woodland and cemetery. However, it only showed possible routes, not whether squirrels actually used them.

The findings suggest that even when paths exist, squirrels may struggle to move freely through the city.

Survival was estimated from the trapping records, which were used to work out the chance of a squirrel still being around six months later.

The chance of surviving six months came to 75% in the woodland, 74% in the cemetery and 69% in the park.

The figure for the park was the lowest of the three. However, the uncertainty around the estimates meant researchers could not establish a clear difference between the sites.

Were more inbred squirrels less likely to survive? If anything, they showed a weak tendency to survive slightly better (the opposite of what had been predicted), though the trend wasn’t statistically significant.

In addition, these survival estimates cannot distinguish between a squirrel that died and one that permanently left the study area.

There were also no measurements of food supply, predators or disease.

Stephanie Kramer-Schadt, who heads the Department of Ecological Dynamics at Leibniz-IZW, supervised the research. She is also a professor at the Technische Universität Berlin (TU Berlin).

The term connectivity is used by scientists for how easily animals can move between patches of habitat.

“The results show that Berlin’s squirrels exhibit a high level of genetic diversity and that there is currently no evidence of significant inbreeding or advanced isolation,” said Kramer-Schadt.

“Should connectivity between urban habitats continue to decline in future, this could also lead to a further reduction in genetic exchange.”

Over many years, even small differences in survival could add up, the authors noted. It isn’t yet known whether that will happen here.

Studies that follow Berlin’s squirrels for longer (and across more of the city) could show whether the genetic split ever affects how long the animals live.

The full study was published in the journal Ecology and Evolution.

The missing 1.2 billion years of geological history at the Grand Canyon finally has an explanation.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

More than a billion years of geological history is missing from the walls of the Grand Canyon, and now, scientists may know why.

In the canyon's sides, ancient metamorphic and igneous rocks that formed 1.7 billion years ago sit directly under younger sedimentary rocks laid down 500 million years ago. The 1.2 billion-year chunk of history in between wasn't preserved — leaving a geological gap known as the Great Unconformity.

This missing period was a very important time in Earth's history, because it was just before and during the Cambrian explosion, which saw a huge diversification of life on Earth. The Great Unconformity is not only at the Grand Canyon; there are big gaps in the rock layers of that time across North America, the Baltic region of Europe and in northern China. Researchers have long debated why this unconformity exists.

The unconformity is sharply evident in the transition between Cambrian Tapeats Sandstone and Proterozoic Brahma Schist in the Grand Canyon.

Now, a new model of the movement of Earth's middle layer, the mantle, has revealed an explanation: The slow, heat-driven circulation of the mantle pushed these three regions upward during the time when the Great Unconformity was formed, according to new research published Nov. 4 in the journal Nature.

This uplift would have helped facilitate erosion, meaning sediments formed at that time sloughed off the continents and landed in the ocean. Importantly, the model also shows that in the past 540 million years, these same areas started sinking instead of rising, creating areas for sediments to get caught and then keep piling up in neat layers on the continents — marking the point where the Great Unconformity ends. This matches what geologists can see in North America, the Baltics and northern China.

"We looked at, where are the best places that the mantle would help create a Great Unconformity?" study co-author Nicolas Flament, a geoscientist at the University of Wollongong in Australia, told Live Science. "And these three places turned out to be three places where it's known to be quite extensive."

Erosion during Neoproterozoic times, followed by sedimentation during early Phanerozoic times, formed the Great Unconformity. Bottom: Dynamic uplift was followed by subsidence for Laurentia ('LAU'), Baltica ('BAL') and North China ('NCH').

The cause of the Great Unconformity is hotly debated, with some arguing that a global deep freeze known as Snowball Earth could have shoveled sediment off the continents in this period. Glaciation probably played a major role in erosion, Flament said, but the new study suggests that the key driver was deep within the planet. Without the mantle pushing the continents upward, glaciers and other erosive forces would have had no slope to push sediments down, he said.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Earth is in a constant state of recycling crust through plate tectonics, said Shanan Peters, a geologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who was not involved in the study. Oceanic crust sinks back into the mantle through the process of subduction ‪—‬ when one tectonic plate dives beneath another. The chemicals it carries down with it get released back into the atmosphere via volcanic eruptions, linking the mantle with the atmosphere.

And tectonics aren't steady. As continents break up and join back together over eons, different materials get pushed into the crust. For example, the ancient Paleo-Tethys ocean, which lapped off the shores of the supercontinent Pangaea until it closed about 200 million years ago, was rich in carbon-bearing sediments that eroded from the continents, Peters said. When the ocean floor was subducted back into the mantle, this carbon was pushed into the depths of the planet.

It contributes to the environment in which complex life evolved.

Today, in contrast, most of Earth's subduction is around the Pacific Rim, and much of the Pacific seafloor is remote from continents, so the seafloor is relatively starved of carbon. What's getting pushed into the mantle now is therefore a different chemical composition than what existed 200 million years ago.

In that sense, referring to the Great Unconformity as "missing information" isn't accurate, Peters told Live Science. Instead, the absence of a rock record in those places at that time reveals something about the processes going on back then — and hints at how geology might have been affecting the atmosphere, and thus life's evolution.

The geological processes occurring during the time of the Great Unconformity may have set the stage for the Cambrian explosion, Peters said. For example, the crystalline rocks exposed on the surface at that time may have released elements like potassium, iron, manganese and carbon into the seas at an increased rate, prompting marine life to invent biomineralization — shells — in response and possibly shifting the composition of Earth's atmosphere to be more oxygen-rich, Peters said.

Flament agreed that the geological changes had significant knock-on effects for life. "It contributes to the environment in which complex life evolved," Flament said.

What's particularly interesting about the Great Unconformity is how it reveals not just a period of erosion but also a switch back to the deposition of sediments. The new paper provides an explanation for both, Peters said, and changes in the mantle are just the planetary-scale process to explain this big-picture phenomenon.

"This seems to me to be the only reasonable way to go back and forth between this state over time," he said.

There are still questions about what else the continents were doing in this time period. Peters leads an effort called Macrostrat that is pulling together observations of rock layers around the world, and Flament said he hopes that database will help ground-truth the new models' findings.

"So far in Africa and Russia, we don’t have as comprehensive a database," he said. "Once that is done, we can go and check whether the idea works."

Editor's Note: This story was updated at 10:30 p.m. E.D.T. to note that James Price, not Tia Ghose, edited this story.

#6349. What’s the Best Snow and Ice Melt? Here’s Why Using Rock Salt Shouldn’t Be Your Default Option.

When you need to keep the driveway ice-free, there’s a wide variety of ice melts to consider.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If the winter weather in recent years hasn’t already been causing some chaos, this year’s Super El Niño isn’t helping. Preparation is key. Setting down a layer of snow and ice melt (i.e., deicers) on your driveway and walkways before a snowstorm hits can save you a lot of time shoveling or snow blowing. But when you walk into the home improvement store, there might be more options than you were prepared for. Don’t worry, with just a little bit of information under your belt, you can choose the best ice melt for the job.

Not all ice melt is created equal. Some melts don’t work as well as others in subzero temperatures and won’t be effective against bonded ice. And some ice melt negatively affects nearby lawns and plants, or causes irritation and health issues for pets. Knowing the difference between the ingredients that power your snow and ice melts is important when choosing the right one for you.

Deicers work by exhibiting one of two thermal reactions: exothermic or endothermic. Exothermic materials, such as sodium chloride and magnesium chloride, release heat when they come into contact with ice or snow. Endothermic materials, such as rock salt and calcium magnesium acetate, absorb heat from their surroundings (such as the sun) and use that heat to melt ice.

Because of this difference, exothermic ice melts perform better in subzero temperatures, and endothermic melts become less effective below 20 degrees Fahrenheit or so, especially at night. However, though exothermic reactions are stronger, they can also be more corrosive and less friendly to plants and animals. Blended melts may offer a good balance, which can help the melt work better in lower temperatures, but also be less corrosive and harmful to pets and plants.

Sometimes referred to as a deicer and often simply called “salt,” ice and snow melts can be made of different chemical compounds or blended to take advantage of their different attributes. This can make some less damaging to pavements or nearby plants. We put together a list of the most typical compounds that you’ll see sold by themselves or in a list of ingredients in blended options, which are the most common types you’ll see at stores.

These are some of the most common types of compounds used for melting ice and snow. Some are sold in their pure form or may be an ingredient in a blended formula.

Exothermic ice melt compounds, such as calcium chloride and magnesium chloride, work better in subzero temperatures because they release heat. If you live in an area where winter temperatures regularly drop below zero, consider one of these types or a blend that contains them.

If your winters are milder and average temperatures tend to hover in the twenties, an endothermic ice melt like rock salt or a urea blend can get the job done. Blended ice melts will often combine exothermic and endothermic compounds to help them perform better in lower temperatures and keep the cost more reasonable. Companies that make these blends will often label the bag with the lowest effective temperature to help you know for sure.

Traditional salts can irritate dog and cat paws, and some of the stronger exothermic compounds that include chlorides can also be irritating or harmful if ingested. The American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (ASPCA) says ingestion can lead to ice melt toxicosis, which can cause vomiting or neurological issues. However, ice melt toxicosis is unlikely to happen from just a few licks; the most serious cause is when a bag of melt is left unattended and ingested by your pet in large amounts.

To help combat this, many brands offer “pet safe” varieties of ice melt, but no blend is truly perfect. These animal-friendly blends tend to eliminate sodium or chloride from the mix, but not all do. The ASPCA recommends using urea-based ice melts, as urea (a compound made of carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen) is the least likely ingredient to cause stomach irritation. Another simple idea, especially in cities and suburbs where there is little control over what ice melt the neighbors use, is to adorn your dog in paw booties before taking a walk.

Ice melts that have high concentrations of salts or chlorides can be problematic for vegetation and the environment in general. According to a study by Penn State Extension, when used in large amounts, simple rock salt (sodium chloride) can injure or kill plants near the treated pavement as it washes away, and further pollute waterways, harming fish and other marine life. Instead, the study notes, a compound like calcium magnesium acetate (CMA), which forgoes the use of chlorides or salts, is a safer option for environmentally sensitive areas. Urea-based ice melts are also a good choice.

Like the pet-friendly varieties of deicers, brands can be very loose with how they market their eco-friendly products, especially with the blends; there’s no guarantee that the one you buy won’t partially contain a compound that is harmful in large quantities. If you want to be as eco-friendly as possible, avoid blends that include chlorides and salts.

If that can’t be avoided, just follow the golden rule of “everything in moderation.” After all, overtreating an area is more likely to damage nearby vegetation—even if you use the more environmentally friendly varieties. If you’re still finding noticeable piles of deicer after the snow and ice are gone, you might be using too much.

Corrosion is a considerable problem caused by deicers. Salt-based melts or brines can penetrate porous stone, freeze, and cause the surface to expand. Meanwhile, chlorides can accelerate the rate of corrosion in metal. The Minnesota Pollution Control Agency noted that acetate-based deicers that don’t use chlorides or salts caused low to moderate levels of corrosion, but again, using any ice melt in moderation will help lower the chance of corrosion to your sidewalks, driveways, and nearby railings.

#6348. Watching a fight may change the brain before the first punch

Male mice learned fighting behaviors by watching others, with brain changes resembling those caused by direct fighting experience.

More than 60 years ago, Albert Bandura showed young children an adult behaving aggressively toward an inflatable doll, and the children went on to behave that way themselves.

Thanks in part to those Bobo doll studies, psychologists treat watching as a form of social learning.

Male mice pick something up from watching, too.

Males that only watched other males fight, and never once joined in, walked into their own first fight acting like animals that had been fighting for eight days.

Watching moved them partway toward experience without any of the risk that comes with it. Their brains had shifted in the same direction as the fighters’ brains, though not as far.

Annegret Falkner and her lab at Princeton sorted male mice into three groups and trained each group for eight days straight, three sessions a day.

The fighters got a smaller, submissive mouse dropped into their own cage for nine minutes at a time. Every session was an easy win.

Observers sat in a clear-walled compartment about 4 by 5 by 7 inches (10 by 13 by 17 cm). The team set it on top of another mouse’s cage, and that mouse fought below.

Cutouts in the barrier let the smell and the sound through. There was no way down.

A third group spent the same minutes with a toy mouse and saw no fighting at all.

Day nine brought the same test for everyone. Each mouse faced three back-to-back rounds of four to five minutes, in its own cage, against an undefeated male with real fighting experience.

Across those rounds, the three groups spent roughly the same amount of time in conflict. What changed was who started it.

Fighters and observers both delivered more attacks that drew no response, and both got going sooner than the toy group. They were also attacked less often. The toy-exposed mice did more fleeing.

Watching changed how the observers approached a fight, even though the groups spent similar amounts of time in conflict.

It gave them the timing and the readiness of a trained fighter without raising how much they fought.

The researchers tracked 15 points on each animal’s body, nose to tail tip, in every video frame.

Then they let software sort the footage into 13 recurring behaviors with no human labels attached.

Observers and fighters spent more of the hard fight in the tight, close-quarters postures that come right before an attack, and less of it hanging back.

The same lab had already tied those proactive postures to resilience in a 2022 study. The order of the behaviors lined up too.

The work was led by Jorge Iravedra-García, a postdoctoral researcher.

“Not only are they emulating some of these behaviors, but the way that they move between these behaviors is also quite similar,” said Iravedra-García.

“When you compute the transitions from aggression behavior one to investigation behavior two, experienced animals behave very similarly to observers in those situations as well.”

A fourth group of five mice watched other males for the same eight days, but those males were only being social. No fighting. In the hard fight, this group behaved more like the toy group than like the observers.

Watching other mice wasn’t the ingredient. Watching them fight was.

The observers also paid close attention, and the team could measure it. A program sorted every moment of video into one of seven behaviors, from grooming to pressing against the barrier with the head turned toward the slits.

That last one, attention, took up more of each session as the eight days went by.

“The observing mice don’t care so much when the fighting animals were just walking around and interacting,” Falkner said. “But we see them orient and attend once attacks start.”

While all of this went on, the team was recording from 12 brain regions at once in every animal.

Two colors did the work. Cells that excite their neighbors were engineered to shine green when active, and cells that quiet their neighbors to shine red.

Twelve optical fibers, each about eight thousandths of an inch across (0.2 mm), carried the light back out.

The moment an attack started, activity rose across most of those regions in the fighters.

Observers showed much the same rise while doing nothing but sitting and looking, and the toy group showed almost none of it. In observers, the response also faded faster.

A 2023 study from Stanford University had found cells in one small spot of the hypothalamus that fire when a mouse attacks and when it watches an attack.

The Princeton team found similar activity patterns across most of the brain regions it monitored.

Dopamine told its own story. In observers, the dopamine signal tracked how fast the attacker lunged and how fast the losing mouse ran.

The watcher was taking in both animals, rather than only the winner.

“Observation’s not a replacement for experience,” Falkner said. “But it gets you part of the way there.”

Many brain cells exist to hold other cells quiet. Researchers call that inhibition, and in these mice it loosened.

In four regions tied to aggression, fighters and observers alike showed weaker activity in those quieting cells during the hard fight than the toy group did.

The excitatory side showed no group difference at all, which points at inhibition as the thing that changed.

So the team put it back. Six observers carried an engineered receptor that let a single injection switch the quieting cells back on in four regions, 30 minutes before the hard fight.

Seven more observers got the injection with no receptor to act on.

The six fought like untrained animals. They delivered fewer attacks and took more, and their behavior slid back toward the mice that had spent eight days with a toy.

The reversal provides evidence that reduced inhibition helped drive the observers’ changed fighting behavior.

Observation did not reproduce every effect of direct fighting experience.

Behaviors that involve direct physical contact changed more after real fighting than after watching, which puts a limit on what observation alone can rewrite.

Every animal in the study was male. What a female mouse takes away from watching two males fight is an open question, and Falkner’s lab is starting there.

Human research has tied exposure to violence to a higher chance of later violence, and the argument over violent media has run for decades.

These mouse experiments cannot settle how exposure to violence affects human behavior.

Falkner’s own reading is that changes like these may suit an animal living with violence and work against one that isn’t. Plenty of brain circuitry works the same way in distant species, and biologists call that conserved.

“I have a hunch that probably some of these circuit changes are conserved in mice and humans,” Falkner said.

Her lab now wants to run the whole thing backwards. The team holds a recording of what an observer’s brain does while it watches a fight.

Falkner would like to play that pattern into a mouse that has never seen one, then put that animal in a fight. That experiment hasn’t been run yet.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

#6347. Flounders reveal an unexpected way of life in a freshwater lake

Flounders in a Finnish lake appear to spend their entire lives in freshwater, raising questions about how they reproduce without the sea.

European flounders swim into river mouths to feed, and biologists have long thought they go back to the sea or to partly salty water to spawn.

In Lake Pulmanki, in the far north of Finland, most of the flounders scientists sampled had hatched in freshwater and stayed there their whole lives.

They’re the first evidence that flounders of this group can complete their life cycle without the sea.

The lake was once a fjord, a long, narrow arm of the Arctic Ocean, and it became a freshwater lake after the last ice age. Today, about 37 miles (60 km) of river separate it from the sea.

Thais Ferreira-Araújo began the work as her graduate thesis at the University of Helsinki.

It grew into a study with co-authors in Finland, Italy, Hong Kong, Portugal, and Australia, and it was published in September.

Paolo Momigliano, an associate professor at the University of Tuscia, helped supervise the thesis.

For a sea fish, coping with water that has almost no salt is one problem, and breeding in it is another.

“This is a striking finding because reproduction poses challenges that go beyond an adult fish’s ability to tolerate freshwater,” Momigliano said.

“In fishes, including flounders, salinity affects whether sperm become motile and how eggs develop and remain suspended in the water.”

Salinity is how salty the water is, and motile sperm are sperm that can swim.

Flounders were first recorded in Lake Pulmanki in the 1970s, and researchers at the time couldn’t say why they were there.

One idea was that the fish swam up from the Barents Sea, the stretch of Arctic Ocean off northern Norway and Russia. They would feed in the lake and then head back to the sea to spawn.

The other idea was that the flounders had adapted to spend their whole lives in freshwater. To tell the two ideas apart, researchers needed to know where each fish had been born.

Ferreira-Araújo’s team looked first at otoliths, small bony structures in a fish’s inner ear that help it sense balance and movement.

As an otolith grows, its chemistry keeps a record of the waters the fish has lived in.

Scientists have used the same kind of record to trace where salmon grew up and how northern pike travel between watersheds.

Researchers studying Baltic cod paired ear-bone chemistry with DNA, and Ferreira-Araújo’s team did the same.

They read the full genomes of flounders from the lake and a few sea sites, looking for stretches of DNA that matched how each fish had used fresh and salt water.

Most of the flounders from Lake Pulmanki had spent their entire lives in freshwater. So the lake’s flounders can produce new generations without any time at sea.

The rest had spent part of their lives in salt water or in brackish water, the partly salty mix found where rivers meet the sea.

Fish with different life histories therefore share one lake. Some had lived only in freshwater, while others had spent time in saltier water.

The team found another surprise in nearby fjords, where most of the flounders sampled had also been born in freshwater, a result the authors didn’t expect.

Across the genome as a whole, flounders born in freshwater and flounders born at sea were only slightly different. But 77 small DNA differences were linked to how a fish had used fresh and salt water. They were scattered over 18 chromosomes and tied to 36 genes.

The same fish tended to carry several of these differences at once, even though they were on separate chromosomes. The researchers suggested that natural selection favored certain combinations of genes.

If so, a flounder probably needs many genes working together to live in freshwater from birth, rather than a single change.

When sea fish settle in freshwater, the freshwater group often stops breeding with its relatives at sea, which is one way new species can form.

The lake’s flounders are still genetically similar to their seagoing relatives. That lets researchers look for the exact traits and genes tied to the move into freshwater.

What researchers still don’t know is how these flounders spawn in the lake at all.

Juha Merilä, a professor at the University of Hong Kong, was another of the thesis supervisors, and he named the problem the team hasn’t solved.

“The next question is how they reproduce successfully under conditions that prevent European flounder from doing so in the rest of its range,” Merilä said.

Answering that question will require studying how the sperm and eggs of these fish behave in freshwater.

The full study was published in the journal Evolution.

#6346. A Lost Landmass Nearly the Size of North America Is Hiding Under the Sea—and It Could Rewrite Human History

A geographer calls it Aquaterra. For 120,000 years, early humans lived there—then the oceans swallowed it.

Several years ago, I travelled to North Carolina as part of a research trip for a story about the famous Lost Colony of Roanoke. Trying to leave no stone unturned, I explored the former colony’s dedicated National Historic Site, poured over archives of antique maps, and even took in a lavish outdoor stage production.

Ultimately, trying to wrangle all the many tendrils of that leviathan proved too unwieldy, and many of the ancillary elements have remained confined to my notebooks. Yet one moment from that trip has never been far from my mind, and it reshaped how I thought about our quest for answers about early human history.

It came about during a conversation with Dr. Eric Klingelhofer, a respected scholar and Vice President for Research with The First Colony Foundation. Dr. Klingelhofer had overseen several excavations that yielded remnants of Roanoke, but he was worried that many once-buried artifacts had already been claimed by a much more powerful force.

“Before my retirement,” he told me, “I attended a UNESCO-backed conference on Bonaire in the Dutch West Indies. These causes, rising sea levels and storm surges, plus coastal overdevelopment, endangered every island, as most prehistoric and early colonial sites lie close to the sea.” As we sat there on tranquil, federally protected land, it was hard for me to feel the urgency at the time, but he stressed that we were in a race against time. “At Fort Raleigh,”—the name the National Parks Service gave the National Historic Site—“coastal erosion has already swallowed up excavation units we had dug in 2007. The rate of loss is about twenty feet in twenty years—and it may be increasing.”

After our conversation, I walked along the island’s shoreline, struck by the thought that although I might be walking the same land as those colonists, the landscape wasn’t really the same. Their shoreline likely sat yards farther out than the one I strolled, and as the water swept that land away, it took with it our chance to learn more about the people who once stood there.

In the study of history, we too often focus on the preservation or replication of what was once on a certain parcel of land, taking it as a given that the land itself stayed constant. We spend all our time debating whether the proverbial Ship of Theseus is still the same after centuries of repairs, never stopping to question if the shoreline of Delos on which he landed still remains.

Yet, recent studies have emerged to remind us that even in the absence of human intervention, the world looked different to the peoples of the past than it does to us today.

The scale of this dilemma, the problem of our submerged history, is far greater than a single island in North Carolina, or a single colony from the 1500s. Our whole understanding of early humankind may be built on faulty ground, due specifically to how much of that ground is now underwater. But don’t let your thoughts drift to that Platonic idea of Atlantis; the proper term, as The Atlantic recently reminded us, is Aquaterra.

In 2014, the geographer Jerome E. Dobson mounted a case for the recognition of a global landmass he dubbed Aquaterra, a term he first proposed in 1999. In “Aquaterra Incognita,” Dobson argued that “all landmasses are defined by time as well as space,” and therefore, since “so little is known about the seacoast where a significant portion of humankind surely dwelled for the better part of 120,000 years,” we should properly recognize and name the 22.5-million-square-kilometer landmass that once hosted the earliest human civilizations.

When we think about the ice ages that have cycled across Earth’s history, we can easily picture the glaciers and ice sheets that formed, but we rarely consider where all that water came from. During an ice age, sea levels drop, exposing land that’s now underwater. As a result, the shorelines early humans knew looked very different from the ones we see today.

The lowlands these glaciers exposed were not bereft of life, either. The ecosystems they once supported varied, from grasslands to wetlands, forests to estuaries. They attracted wildlife, and later, early human civilizations. “Compare the most recent curve of sea level rise against the timeline of cultural innovations,” Dobson writes, “and you will find that much human progress occurred while seacoasts were still quite low.”

When the glaciers melted and sea levels rose again, naturally, early humans abandoned their soon-to-be-submerged settlements. But that doesn’t mean we should simply ignore what once stood there. “It would not change the timeline of human progress if, for instance, cities were found as low as -50 meters, since Jericho is known to have existed when sea levels were that low,” Dobson notes. What could revise that timeline, he notes, is “the possibility that precursors of major innovations may exist at even lower depths.”

“One intriguing possibility is pottery,” he proposes:

All this talk about “possibility,” of course, makes the benefits of recognizing Aquaterra seem entirely theoretical. Yet in just the last few years, the archeological world received a stirring reminder that the land we can see is not the only land there ever was, and that whole chapters of our history may have been claimed by the sea.

In 2021, Michael K. Faught and Morgan F. Smith published “The magnificent seven: Marine submerged precontact sites found by systematic geoarchaeology in the Americas.” The study documented not one or two but seven projects, in North America alone, that had found traces of precontact life now drowned beneath the continental shelf. Each of the seven projects worked “from the terrestrially known, to the submerged unknown.” Using methodical but varied mapping and modeling techniques, researchers predicted where people might once have lived, then searched for proof with underwater surveys, sediment cores, and even hands-on excavations.

One of the research efforts happened in the Gulf of Mexico’s paleo-Sabine River. Over the course of a decade, from 1976 to 1986, it turned up “charred wood and vegetation, nut hulls, seeds, fish scales, and bone from fish, reptiles, birds, and small mammals,” some of which dated back 9,000 years. Soon after, researchers in Belize found the drowned outlines of pole-and-thatch buildings, which turned out to be Classic-period Maya salt works now sitting underwater. Other research discussed in the study uncovered stone tools, campsites, and even a stone artifact more than 12,000 years old.

To truly understand human history, we can’t keep digging only in the land we can see. We also have to search for the land our ancestors knew, much of which now lies beneath the waves. That calls for a change in mindset and a rethinking of how archaeology works. As seas keep rising, how many more once-inhabited places will slip beneath the surface, taking with them secrets as recent as Roanoke’s? If we don’t change course now, the sites we have yet to excavate may be written off by tomorrow’s scholars as mere seafloor.

Michale Natale is a News Editor for the Hearst Enthusiast Group. As a writer and researcher, he has produced written and audio-visual content for more than fifteen years, spanning historical periods from the dawn of early man to the Golden Age of Hollywood. His stories for the Enthusiast Group have involved coordinating with organizations like the National Parks Service and the Secret Service, and travelling to notable historical sites and archaeological digs, from excavations of America’ earliest colonies to the former homes of Edgar Allan Poe.
